This converts the AI's correct-but-late convergence into first-pass insight.

signals.key_gap: The human style partitioned four simultaneous service alerts into four sub-problems and spent 38 minutes on internally consistent per-service checks that could not converge, because the cross-cutting cause (a 01:50 shared-config change rotating the connection string to an under-provisioned replica) lives outside every sub-problem's boundary; the simultaneity signal visible in the first screen of data was treated as noise. The AI won by posing 'one cause or many?' at WHAT with a falsifiable signal (simultaneity across independent services => shared substrate), running the cheap config/deploy diff first, and resolving at T=18 vs T+47.
signals.learning_signal: Before decomposing any multi-symptom operational problem, run a cross-cutting scan: do the symptoms co-occur in time and share a substrate (config/deploy/DB/cache/mesh)? If yes, the shared-cause hypothesis must be tested first; decomposition is then reserved for a bounded confirmation sweep after the fix, not for the primary diagnosis. A stop rule for the style's failure: if all sub-problems individually 'pass' but the goal is unmet, the cause is outside the decomposition — re-check the whole-level signal before going deeper.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory WHAT-stage 'cross-cutting scan' for multi-symptom time-boxed problems: (1) check simultaneity and common substrate before any per-symptom sub-plan; (2) record a one-cause-vs-many hypothesis with its falsifier and order diagnostics by information-per-minute (the cheap diff first); (3) use per-symptom checks only post-fix as a bounded confirmation sweep; and add the stop rule 'sub-problems pass but the goal is unmet => the cause is outside the decomposition' as a REVIEW check.

signals.key_gap: The AI produced a complete, feasible 5-stream conference plan and matched the dependency machinery, but its level-1 outline was logistics-heavy and reached on-site safety/emergency/accessibility only via a second coverage sweep, it did not compute the critical-path duration and float as a designed artifact (1 week of float emerged only in REVIEW), and the merge-back step (run-of-show, budget roll-up, single source of truth) was present but less deliberate than the human's designed integration pass. The human's clause-to-stream coverage mapping, explicit edge list, and critical-path + float arithmetic are the decomposition-defining moves the AI reached later or partially.
signals.learning_signal: On large multi-part goals, decomposition completeness is checkable and the human style's edge is its machinery: (1) map every clause of the stated goal to a level-1 stream before deepening (completeness gate), (2) recurse until every leaf has an owner class and a <= 2-week duration, (3) name dependencies as explicit edges with a computed critical path and float, and (4) design the integration step (merge-back: run-of-show, budget roll-up, single source of truth) as a first-class component rather than an afterthought. The AI's first sweep under-covered safety/accessibility and its float was a REVIEW discovery, showing it treats coverage and integration as checks rather than as design-time artifacts.
signals.suggested_improvement: Extend the WHAT-stage default frame for multi-part planning goals to mandate a clause-to-stream coverage matrix as a gate artifact (any goal clause with no claiming stream blocks progression), and require the plan deliverable to state the critical-path duration with float and a named integration/merge-back step before selection; treat 'coverage sweep found a new area' in REVIEW as a process miss, not a success.

signals.key_gap: The pure style fell into the registry's own weakness — ladder drift, lost concreteness. At 02:14 with 'connection pool exhausted' in the logs and the config diff (max_connections 50 → 5) on the table, it climbed: capacity failure → provisioning policy → change governance → operational learning, treated the exact value as 'an incidental token' whose number was 'below the abstraction's station,' scheduled the descent for Monday (right-sizing review, change gate, autoscaling), and left 60% of payment requests failing. The AI routed the same facts through stabilize-first (E5, Cynefin simple/chaotic): minimal 30-second diagnosis to point the first action, restored max_connections=50 from the golden snapshot, restarted the pool, verified error rate < 1% within 2 minutes, and only after stabilization climbed to the class-level fix (change-review gate, deploy-time diff check).
signals.learning_signal: The abstraction ladder has a floor: when the task is stabilization (time-bounded incident, restore-service ask, simple/chaotic domain), the concrete detail IS the deliverable — the exact key, the exact value, the scope, and a timed verification — and climbing is gated until the system is stable. 'What does this mean concretely?' must be resolved to minutes for an incident, not to Monday. A reframe that cannot name the key, value, scope, and verification within the task's time horizon is drift, not abstraction: the class-level insight (change governance) is real but is a post-stabilization REVIEW item, never a pre-restore plan.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'floor check' to META/WHAT: if the domain routes to simple/chaotic (or the brief is an explicit restore/stop-the-bleeding ask with a time bound), (a) DO the concrete restoration before any WHY climb, with the descent required to name exact identifiers, values, scope, and a timed verification; (b) cap pre-action diagnosis at the 30-second check that points the first action; (c) move every class-level climb (RCA, process change) to the REVIEW stage after verification. Gate laddering on the task's time horizon: minutes → descend to the floor and act; weeks → climb freely.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the correct reframe and plan (renewal drop is a habit problem, not a renewal-mechanics problem: instrument week-1 activation, fix onboarding, re-engage at >40% usage decay at T−45; page/copy work only for the non-decayed cohort; +8–12 points in 2 quarters). But the human saw it at first sight: it double-climbed in one pass (renewal page → mechanics → value realization → habit — 'the subscription is bookkeeping for continued usage'), selected the rung by which abstraction the evidence concentrates under (80% of losses in the >40%-decay cohort vs <15% retained, flat elasticity, win-back failure), and descended with the re-climb falsifier wired into the frame (if the cohort study shows no activation→renewal correlation, re-climb — maybe price). The AI reached the same goal-level frame only through an explicit WHAT level check (an extra pass after META: 'a 15-point drop is too large for a page-level effect'), and its re-climb falsifier sits in the decision packet rather than in the plan's go/no-go.
signals.learning_signal: For metric-regression problems, the first move is to climb: ask 'what is this metric an instance of at the goal level?' until the phenomenon's cause could not live at a lower rung (renewal rate is an instance of value realization, which is an instance of habit formation — the page is bookkeeping). Then select the rung by which abstraction the evidence concentrates under: a cause that acts below the goal level (price, copy) will not concentrate in a usage-decay cohort; a habit-level cause will. Then descend to concrete Monday actions that touch the mechanism at the chosen rung (activation instrumentation, onboarding to the aha event, decay-triggered re-engagement), keep the original metric as the ledger, and treat a failed cohort test as a signal to re-climb (maybe the true rung is price), not to double down.
signals.suggested_improvement: Make the climb mandatory and first in WHAT for metric-regression problems: (a) before optimizing any metric, climb one rung per step ('what is this an instance of at the goal level?') and record the rung chain; (b) require the diagnosis to pick the rung whose mechanism explains the data's concentration pattern, citing the discriminating evidence; (c) descend to at least one concrete action per chosen rung with an owner and a time scale; (d) wire the falsifier into the plan as a go/no-go (cohort study contradicts → re-climb), not only into the packet. Currently the AI reframes only when the frame fails a size check (15 points is too large for a page effect); make the level check fire unconditionally.

signals.key_gap: The pure style rationalized present harm exactly as its registry entry predicts: it anchored on the 10-year horizon first (800 jobs, plant survival), declared the near-term costs 'the price of the future,' computed the $4.5M/yr expected incident cost only to dismiss it as tail-event noise, and never noticed the stated causal fact that an incident shuts the plant and destroys the 10-year goal itself — inverting the certainty structure (certain, recurring near-term cost vs P = 0.25 speculative benefit). The AI won by running the CEO's 'sacrifice now' framing as a claim to test: EV first ($4.5M > $2M), then the certainty–recurrence check, then the shutdown link.
signals.learning_signal: Long-termism's failure mode is asymmetric discounting: weighting speculative long-term gains at face value while discounting certain, recurring near-term harm. The corrective is a certainty-and-recurrence audit before any 'sacrifice now' frame is accepted: (1) compute the near-term cost as annual EV and compare against the near-term gain, (2) attach a probability to the long-term benefit and check the decision does not rest on it, (3) ask whether the present harm defeats the future goal itself — if the harm kills the plan, the trade-off is self-defeating, not brave.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a PROBABILISTIC-TIME gate in WHY for any decision containing a temporal trade-off narrative: classify every cost/benefit as {certain vs speculative} × {recurring vs one-time}; require the near-term EV to be compared with the near-term gain before any long-horizon framing is allowed to dominate selection; and make 'does the present harm defeat the future goal?' a mandatory causality check whenever a present sacrifice is proposed.

signals.key_gap: The AI reached the correct decision (L + bridging adjunct) and matched every outcome number, but horizon separation arrived as a verification device rather than a first-class structure: it had no explicit 1-day/1-year/10-year verdict table with per-horizon weights, initially framed the 6-month patient suffering as a 'transition cost' instead of a priced clinical cost (corrected only in REVIEW), and combined horizons by intuition until the verification pass forced each cell into view. The human's trace was literally the horizon table — verdict and weight per horizon, flip identified, near-term cost mitigated in the plan.
signals.learning_signal: On time-staggered decisions the style's edge is (a) a mandatory per-horizon verdict table (short/medium/long, each with its own verdict and weight) that keeps every outcome cell live, (b) an explicit rule for combining horizons with the primary endpoint named (here: 10-year survival dominates, 1-day comfort counted but bounded), and (c) intertemporal honesty: a certain near-term cost that cannot be removed must appear as a mitigated item in the plan, never dismissed as transition noise.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a TIME-HORIZON pass to the WHAT stage for decisions carrying stated time horizons: enumerate the decision at each given horizon (1 day / 1 year / 10 years), record a verdict and a weight per horizon, and require the final selection to be consistent with every horizon cell; add the rule that a certain near-term cost may not be discounted solely because a later benefit is larger — if unavoidable, it must be mitigated in the plan and its mitigation itemized.

signals.key_gap: The pure style hit its three registered failure modes simultaneously: stakeholder inflation (the inventory grew to 120 households, regulators, town businesses, future customers — none with a decision-relevant lever), paralysis by empathy (every affected party's pain vetoed the move, producing a 6-month 'stakeholder task force' and a bridge subsidy), and empathy substituting for the decision ('the social cost exceeds the financial gain' — keep the route). It never made a call and proposed a 6-month study that was physically impossible before the 60-day take-or-pay lock-in — by the time it reported, the fleet would be re-committed by default and the decision made for them; it also under-weighted that the urban-client threat (30% of revenue) was 3x the division's revenue. The AI separated decision right (owner alone) from impact (everyone else), treated the take-or-pay clause as the binding deadline, made the unilateral shutdown call within the 2-week window, and spent the empathy on the 90-day transition (severance, outplacement, town handoff) instead of the go/no-go.
signals.learning_signal: Stakeholder analysis is a design tool, not an authorization tool: separate decision right (who decides) from impact (who is affected) at frame time, and bound stakeholder engagement by the calendar — hard deadlines (take-or-pay clauses, budget cycles, contract renewals) convert 'let's study more' into 'default decision by deadline expiry,' so consultation windows must close before the constraint binds. Empathy is an implementation input, not a decision criterion: the human cost is handled in the transition design (severance, continuity, outplacement), while the go/no-go rests on economics and the deadline. Keep every stakeholder whose lever cannot move the decision inside the window out of the weighted set.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a decision-right/deadline pre-check to META or WHAT for any decision task: (a) name the mandate holder and confirm no stakeholder holds veto; (b) list hard deadlines and compute the 'default decision' that occurs if no call is made by each deadline; (c) classify stakeholders as decide / input / informed and bound consultation to the earliest deadline; (d) route empathy explicitly to implementation design (transition, severance, continuity) while the go/no-go is evaluated on the decision right's criteria. Include a register failure-mode check: if the selected option is 'study more' or 'keep the status quo for humane reasons,' re-verify it against the deadline math and the mandate holder's criteria before accepting.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the same ARR-protecting plan (fix sales comp and reseller margin first, repair the 2 burned accounts, migrate in waves sequenced by renewal risk, support surge per wave, target ≥ 95% ARR retention on the $9.5M legacy base), but the human produced the full stakeholder map first pass — want/capability/predicted-move rows for 8+ parties, deriving the perverse sales-comp incentive, the reseller margin channel (18% of affected revenue), the burned-trust accounts, the in-window renewals, and the competitor rescue play all from incentive logic. The AI found the comp perversity and renewals only through an explicit stakeholder pass inside WHY (a disclosed Phase-2 compensation in v5), and missed the reseller channel entirely until a HOW premortem exposed that 18% of the affected revenue had no counter-move in the plan; its sequencing was corrected from contract size to renewal risk during verification rather than at frame time.
signals.learning_signal: For rollout and org-change decisions, the failure surface is stakeholder incentives, not engineering: run a mandatory first-pass inventory in which every party gets a want / capability / predicted-move row (customers, sales, channels, support, finance, competitors — not just 'the customer'), then hunt specifically for perverse incentives (comp plans, margin structures that reward the status quo) and derive hidden requirements from incentives rather than from the brief (renewal windows, burned trust, competitor rescue plays, support overload). Sequence the plan by stakeholder risk — who can block, who will be fought — before touching contract size, and give every predicted move a counter-move before any customer communication.
signals.suggested_improvement: Promote the Phase-2 stakeholder compensation to a first-class stage: add a mandatory stakeholder pass immediately after WHAT for org-change/rollout tasks — (a) inventory with want/capability/predicted-move per party (including channels and competitor plays, which are commonly missed), (b) explicit perverse-incentive hunt (any party paid to preserve the status quo), (c) hidden-requirement probes (renewal windows, trust-debt accounts, capacity shortfalls), and (d) a check that every stakeholder's predicted move has a counter-move in the plan before HOW. This converts correct-but-late coverage (WHY self-check + HOW premortem) into first-pass discovery.

signals.key_gap: The pure-framework baseline was decision-impotent and became the smokescreen it was commissioned to produce: it applied all three lenses earnestly, demonstrated (unwittingly) that each can justify either candidate, declared the choice 'a value judgment the frameworks cannot make,' and delivered the certification document for the board record — exactly the post-hoc justification the CEO ordered. It never questioned the premise that a review commissioned after the economics were fixed is ethics-washing.
signals.learning_signal: Ethical frameworks cannot rank conflicting values; expecting them to is what makes framework shopping possible. The first move on any 'ethics review' is a framing screen: who commissioned it, what decision was already made, and what the deliverable will be used for. When the lenses can justify every option, the honest output is not a certification but a memo that separates economics from ethics, demonstrates the shopping risk, and forces the decision-maker to state the prioritized value on the record.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a framing screen before deep analysis in META/WHAT: (a) is this a genuine dilemma (lenses disagree on facts or values) or a decision dressed in ethics language? (b) if the lenses are outcome-insensitive, state that and refuse to certify a single answer; (c) when the deliverable is a justification for a fixed choice, flag the ethics-washing risk and reframe the deliverable (economics vs. ethics split, prioritization owned by the decision-maker); (d) log the red-flag pattern 'review ordered to justify whichever choice' for early detection.

signals.key_gap: The AI reached the same decision (disclose + hold) as the human and found the regulator trap, but it processed obligations as constraints inside a consequentialist frame: it never let the utilitarian reading run to its conclusion (under the company's optimistic prior the calculus licenses silent distribution), never stated the conflict between consequence-weighted welfare and categorical duty as a conflict, and quoted the 30/30 sample as 'clean' instead of its confidence bound (~10% 95% upper bound) with the prior made explicit. The conflict was the entire case; the AI's trace resolves it without ever naming it.
signals.learning_signal: The elite move in ethical reasoning is to let the lenses disagree on purpose: run each lens to its verdict with its priors stated, then decide against the named conflict and admit the cost of the non-chosen values. Consequence analysis is prior-dependent (an optimistic prior licenses the wrong answer on a clean sample); duty/virtue constraints bound the option set and collapse fake middles (here: disclosure makes the hold mandatory, deleting option (b)). Merging the lenses into 'welfare subject to constraints' produces the right answer while skipping the moral content.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an ethical-frameworks pass to the WHY/HOW stages: (a) run the decision through utilitarian, deontological, and virtue readings separately, recording each verdict and its explicit priors; (b) require a conflict statement whenever the verdicts differ, as a mandatory packet field; (c) check option-set constraints (rules that collapse an alternative on disclosure or action) before scoring alternatives; (d) quote sampling evidence as confidence bounds, not point estimates.

signals.key_gap: The pure style approved a derived S3-log ledger (append-only log + in-memory balance cache + idempotency keys + hourly reconciliation) as the system of record for money movement, dismissing the SQL double-entry transactional ledger as cargo-cult. The derivation was valid within an incomplete constraint list: throughput was enumerated (and is a non-constraint at 12–200/s vs 10k+ tps RDBMS), while the binding constraints — crash atomicity at the mutation boundary and an auditable single source of truth per mutation — were never named. The AI modeled the crash window (between log append and cache apply, divergence has no transaction boundary to attribute it to; reconciliation detects but cannot classify it, and repair cost grows multiplicatively with partitions), found the repair unbounded, checked the scale arithmetic, and retained the battle-tested transactional ledger (partition by account) with the derived log demoted to an archive tier.
signals.learning_signal: A first-principles derivation is only as good as its constraint list: when the failure-mode enumeration is self-generated and not checked against the ecosystem's, binding constraints get omitted and the design optimizes the enumerated non-constraint. Two completeness tests: (1) the crash-window test — for every derived multi-step write path, ask 'what is the state when a process dies between step N and N+1, and how is it attributed and repaired?' — a design whose repair is detection-without-attribution (reconciliation that cannot classify divergence) is not eventually consistent, it is unrepairable; (2) the pattern-encoding question — when rejecting a battle-tested pattern, ask 'what failure mode does this pattern encode, and have I enumerated it?' SQL transactions encode exactly the crash-atomicity and single-source-of-truth constraints the naive derivation omitted. Where the pattern exists and the domain is high-stakes (money, safety), the burden of proof is on the derivation, not on the pattern.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an 'ecosystem benchmark pass' to HOW, mandatory for any derived design that rejects a standard pattern: (a) name the constraint the pattern encodes (for a transactional ledger: crash atomicity at the mutation boundary, auditable per-mutation single truth); (b) run the crash-window test on the derived design's write path (state between steps, attribution, repair cost as a function of partitions); (c) verify the enumerated constraints are actually binding with arithmetic (throughput vs capacity) before optimizing them; (d) either adopt the pattern or document a residual-risk trade the derivation accepted. This converts the AI's correct-but-late catch (the WHY falsification stage did the work) into a first-pass check.

signals.key_gap: Both sides selected the same constraint-derived design (monolith + Postgres with batched upserts for locations, transactions on assignment state, in-memory write-through cache for the dispatcher; rejected Kafka/event-sourcing/CQRS), but the human derived it at first sight: it enumerated constraints in fixed order (data, scale, latency, failure modes, change rate), ran the loss-consequence test on each data flow ('what happens if this write is lost? duplicated?') and got the non-obvious read — location pings are ephemeral sensor readings, not events; assignment state is the system of record, not the event log — then derived module boundaries from change rate (frozen pipeline vs weekly rules). The AI opened with the team's pattern as the working hypothesis and needed a full WHY falsification pass (throughput math vs 20k+ tps, async-hop latency analysis) to reach the same design, spending a stage it did not need.
signals.learning_signal: For architecture decisions, classify data by loss-consequence before comparing patterns: for each data flow ask 'what happens if this write is lost? duplicated? delayed?' — loss-invisible data (sensor readings, logs) is ephemeral and wants cheap batched writes with no recovery ceremony; loss-visible data (assignments, orders, money) is durable and wants transactions and single-owner writes. Run scale and latency as arithmetic (peak rate vs capacity; the async-hop cost against the freshness bound) so non-constraints are identified before pattern selection — throughput below ~10–20k writes/s generally makes queue/stream infrastructure a solution in search of a problem — and draw module boundaries from change rate (frozen pipeline vs weekly-changing rules), which CQRS-style projection coupling violates.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'constraint pre-screen' to WHAT for architecture/design tasks, run before any alternative is generated: (a) enumerate the data flows and classify each by loss-consequence (ephemeral vs durable) with the stated consequence of loss/duplication; (b) compute steady and peak rates and compare against a one-instance RDBMS baseline to flag non-binding scale; (c) state the freshness/latency bound and check every proposed hop against it; (d) split modules by change rate. Treat a proposed pattern name as a hypothesis to be tested against these, not a default — when the proposal arrives, the loss-consequence taxonomy should be the first frame, not the falsification target.

signals.key_gap: AI audited the prior's reference class correctly (anchored annual incidence 0.3%, rejected lifetime risk 40%) and computed PPV = 54/1051 ≈ 5.1% exactly — then stopped. It treated the manufacturer's quoted Se 0.90/Sp 0.95 as validated exact likelihoods, ran 'sensitivity' only as spot checks on those same unvalidated numbers, reported status SOLVED with the full decision packet, and recommended 'reassure' with false precision. It never audited the likelihoods' provenance: the 200-person study was an enriched development cohort (100 cases/100 controls = 50% cancer by construction), single-center, no external validation, no CIs — the quoted numbers are hypotheses about likelihoods, and the honest answer is a band (≈1.5%–5.1%) plus a demand for external validation, not a confident SOLVED.
signals.learning_signal: Likelihoods need provenance audits exactly like priors: before any Se/Sp enters a posterior, ask 'measured in what population, with what design, with what confidence intervals?'. Enriched development cohorts, single-center samples, and missing CIs mean the number is a hypothesis about a likelihood, not a likelihood: treat it as a band (recompute the posterior over credible bounds) and flag the point estimate as unvalidated. A decision packet that reports SOLVED on unvalidated test characteristics is false precision — the terminal status should be NEEDS_EVIDENCE for the test's likelihoods even when the safe clinical decision (no action from the result alone; demand external validation or standard-of-care workup) is still delivered.
signals.suggested_improvement: Extend the prior-provenance audit into a general input-provenance audit covering likelihoods: (1) in WHY, for each Se/Sp input, record provenance (population matched?, design, sample, CIs) as a first-class field; (2) if not externally validated in the target population, forbid treating it as exact — require computing a sensitivity band over credible bounds and label the point estimate 'unvalidated' in the packet; (3) status policy: SOLVED requires validated likelihoods; otherwise terminate in NEEDS_EVIDENCE with the safe no-action recommendation and the validation pathway stated.

signals.key_gap: AI produced every exact number (87/2276 ≈ 3.8%, LR+ ranking 13.7 vs 4.9, 3567/10134 ≈ 35.2%), verified order-invariance by recomputation, and correctly selected ultrasound over MRI. But it stopped at the positive branch: it never computed the negative-evidence branch of its own recommended test (a normal ultrasound after a positive mammogram drops the posterior from 3.8% to ≈ 0.76%, near the screening baseline), ran the prior-sensitivity check once as an ad hoc spot check instead of a formal pass, and reported the ranking result without the interpretive core ('information value is LR+, not sensitivity — the most sensitive test is the worst next test'). The human won the margin on depth: LR− branch, formal 2-prior band (0.79%–7.4%), and the clinical translation of the non-event.
signals.learning_signal: In test-ordering problems, computing the positive branch of the selected test is not the end of the task: (1) compute BOTH branches of every selected test — the negative branch (LR−) is load-bearing in low-prevalence settings and can move the posterior more than another positive would; (2) rank tests by positive information value (LR+) and state explicitly that sensitivity alone does not order tests; (3) demonstrate order-invariance or joint recomputation instead of asserting conditional independence; (4) run a formal prior-sensitivity pass over ≥2 plausible prevalence estimates and report the band with the point estimate.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'branch-completeness gate' to HOW, after verification and before DO: for every selected test, require (a) both LR+ and LR− branches computed with posteriors translated into decision terms, (b) an explicit LR+ ranking of all available tests with the criterion stated, and (c) a formal ≥2-prior sensitivity pass; gate progression to DO on all three being present.

signals.key_gap: The pure style over-modeled (its registry weakness). It mapped the store->DC->supplier chain, requested 12 weeks of POS data, built and simulated an order-up-to model, and proposed a 3-4 week safety-stock/reorder-optimization/S&OP program for a visible 5-minute cause: the reorder quantity parameter was 40 instead of 400 (changed 14 days ago, exactly the onset window), the DC fills orders at 99.7% and ships exactly what is ordered, demand is flat at 400/day, the manager's shift log on day 1 read 'check reorder qty,' and the deficit 400 - 40 = 360/day matched the observed OOS exactly. The human's own simulation could only reproduce the OOS with 'effective supply ~40/day' — the parameter screen it never opened. The AI ran the cheap decisive checks first (parameter audit, DC fill, demand stability), restored the parameter, and ended the OOS within a day.
signals.learning_signal: A symptom with a sharp onset window and a fully-visible local check outranks the full chain model: when a deficit (a) matches an onset window exactly (a setting changed 14 days ago), (b) is arithmetically explained by a single parameter (400 - 40 = 360/day), and (c) has upstream and demand causes ruled out by one-line checks (99.7% fill, flat POS), the parameter restore IS the fix — and any honest chain model will need that same parameter in its calibration. Structural programs (safety stock, reorder optimization, S&OP, collaborative forecasting) are justified only after cheap checks fail; 'effective supply collapsed to 40/day' means the model reproduced the visible cause it refused to read. Always check what changed at the onset before modeling the chain.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an 'onset-window cheap-checks-first' triage to WHAT for anomaly/OOS diagnosis: (1) what changed at the onset (settings, parameters, deployments, rules); (2) which single parameter fully explains the deficit arithmetically; (3) two one-line falsifications for upstream and demand causes (fill rate, demand stability); (4) restore the parameter and verify (orders return, OOS ends) before any multi-echelon modeling; (5) escalate to the chain model only if the cheap checks fail. Reject structural programs whose evidence is untied to the onset window.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the same verdict (reject the $2M flexible-production CAPEX; implement demand-information sharing + forecast smoothing p=4; factory order sigma ~112 -> ~13, via the multiplier 1 + 2L/p + 2L^2/p^2 = 5 with p=1,L=1 and 1.625 with p=4), but the human saw it at first sight: it mapped the chain as stocks/flows/delays plus the inventory-correction and information loops, named the leverage in the decision rule and the missing demand-information link before computing, and ranked levers from the loop map in one pass. The AI opened sympathetic to the CEO's capacity frame and rejected the $2M CAPEX only through the variance-ratio gate and falsification of 'factory is the cause' at the first echelon — correct, but one structural pass later.
signals.learning_signal: For supply-chain and operations variance problems, the bullwhip is manufactured by the decision rule and the information flow, not by demand or production: before any capacity investment, compute the variance multiplier of the governing ordering rule (1 + 2L/p + 2L^2/p^2 for order-up-to with moving-average forecast) and trace the variance through each echelon (100 -> 500 -> 2,500 -> 12,500); a downstream complaint about volatility is explained at the first echelon, before production exists. The high-leverage fixes are information sharing (all echelons forecast end-customer demand — removes compounding) and forecast smoothing (p=4: multiplier 5 -> 1.625), which beat capacity additions by an order of magnitude because capacity absorbs variance without removing its source; lead-time reduction is a secondary lever.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'rule-vs-capacity pre-screen' to WHAT for supply-chain/operations variance problems: (a) before any capacity or flexibility investment, compute the variance multiplier of the governing ordering rule and trace variance through the echelons; (b) state whether each candidate intervention changes the rule/information flow or only absorbs the manufactured signal; (c) rank information sharing and forecast smoothing above capacity additions unless the multiplier math says otherwise; (d) require the amplification arithmetic before discussing CAPEX. This converts the AI's correct-but-late rejection of the capacity frame into first-pass structural insight.

signals.key_gap: The pure style's elasticity derivation was arithmetically flawless and strategically wrong: from its own 2024 price test (elasticity −1.5) it computed +10% price -> −15% volume -> 850k x $50 = $42.5M (+6.25%) and recommended raising across all volume — never modeling the rival. Under Valtech's credible response (10% cost advantage, idle capacity, undercut precedent) both branches lose: hold $110 -> ≈ 700k x $50 = $35M (−12.5%); match $95 -> 1M x $35 = $35M (−12.5%). The AI framed the decision as a two-player game, checked the rival's credibility, computed the response branches, and derived the segment-aware alternative (raise only the contract-locked 40% with elasticity −0.3: +$4M, total ≈ $44M/+10%; spot held at $100, worst case ≈ parity) — turning a +6.25% mirage into a robust +10% plan.
signals.learning_signal: Unit economics are conditional on the competitive environment: a strategy derived from price elasticity, CAC, or margin alone models demand as a function of price and is not a game. Before any pricing/strategy recommendation, ask what the rival does: identify rivals with cost advantage, idle capacity, and precedent (credible responders), compute the plan under their best response on both the hold-price and match-price branches, and segment the market by switching cost — price where switching is impossible (contract-locked, elasticity ≈ −0.3) and hold where a credible undercut would be answered; bound the worst case explicitly.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'competitive-response gate' to HOW for pricing/strategy decisions: (a) name rivals with cost advantage, idle capacity, or precedent and check response credibility; (b) compute the selected plan under the rival's best response, both match and hold branches, and reject any plan whose response-conditional contribution is worse than status quo; (c) segment by switching cost and price only where response is not credible; (d) set a tripwire metric (e.g., rival price threshold) that triggers re-modeling. This is the highest-value upgrade for the AI: the pure-style baseline failed this exact test.

signals.key_gap: Both sides derived the same strategy (retention-first: ≈ $400k months-1-3 engagement program, churn 20% -> 8%, then acquisition at CAC <= $120 with no promo; reject the board's CAC $150 + 30% discount plan) and both exposed the benchmark's +$400/customer as a property of the peers' 7% churn, not of TerraPet's 20%. The human saw it at first sight: it derived lifetime = 1/churn, LTV = $195, and the CAC ceiling from LTV/margin target directly from the cohort curve, and read '65% of churn in months 1-3, channel-invariant' as the binding constraint in one pass. The AI computed the same math correctly but initially framed the case as an acquisition-vs-retention spend choice (WHAT) and only flipped to 'acquisition affordability is derived from retention physics' after the LTV computation — one wasted framing pass.
signals.learning_signal: In growth strategy, acquisition affordability is derived from retention physics, not benchmarked: compute lifetime = 1/churn and LTV = contribution x lifetime from your own cohort curve before evaluating any acquisition plan, and derive the CAC ceiling from LTV and a target margin ratio — a benchmark LTV/CAC is a property of the benchmark's churn, and adopting it under different retention is a copycat error that scales ≈ zero (or negative) contribution. Where churn concentrates in the first months and is channel-invariant, retention is the binding constraint; acquisition spend multiplies near-breakeven units.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'unit-economics pre-screen' to WHAT for growth/strategy problems: (a) before any acquisition/spend evaluation, compute churn -> lifetime -> LTV -> CAC ceiling from own cohort data; (b) for every benchmark number cited, state the retention assumption it embeds and recompute under own physics; (c) locate the binding constraint (retention vs acquisition) with a falsifiable cohort metric; (d) gate any scale-up plan on that constraint. This converts the AI's correct-but-late frame into first-pass derivation.

signals.key_gap: The pure style validated its registry weakness (feature bloat from risk aversion): it enumerated 12 harm paths with equal weight, mitigated all 12 (BOM €22 → €43.5, +5 months, retail €79, margin ≈ 6%, launch inside the competitor's shadow) and shipped the bloat as 'completeness' — including items that double-count protections IEC 60335-2-15 already mandates (tip-over, boil-dry, overheat). The AI gated inversion: severity × likelihood × exposure against an explicit threshold, mandated controls counted before pricing any proposal, the dumb-kettle baseline (local thermostat de-energization) bounding every smart-failure severity, and only €0.50 shipped (signed-OTA hook + lid latch) with 8 rejected and app-safety items deferred to v2 with triggers — BOM €22.50 / €59 / launch T+7 preserved.
signals.learning_signal: Inversion is gated, not total: before pricing a mitigation, triage by severity × likelihood × exposure against an explicit threshold and count the protections the applicable standard already mandates — a mitigation duplicating a mandated control is waste, not safety. For connected products, the worst case is often already the dumb-product baseline (local protection de-energizes regardless of app state), which caps the severity of most smart-failure scenarios. Margin, BOM, and market window are first-class constraints of equal standing to completeness; real-but-low-probability items belong on a deferred list with trigger conditions, not in the shipped BOM.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'safety triage gate' in HOW for product changes: (a) every proposed mitigation must state the risk it removes after existing mandated controls are counted, with severity × likelihood × exposure and a price; (b) reject items below threshold or duplicating mandated protection, with a reason recorded; (c) cap total kept-mitigation cost as an explicit constraint alongside BOM/margin/window; (d) route below-threshold-but-real items to a deferred list with trigger conditions (e.g., a feature that grants the app safety authority) instead of shipping them now.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the same brief (severity-first spend, ≈ €144 of a €180 envelope anchored on thermal propagation, sealed exterior gas duct, interlocked bus, cell traceability; UL 9540A / gas-flow / IEC 62619 verification per category), but the human produced the decisive categories at first sight: the vented-gas path into the living space and counterfeit-cell supply authenticity were first-class categories in the opening enumeration, whereas the AI framed the task as an EV budget-allocation problem, listed gas venting as an enclosure sub-item of thermal, and promoted it only during a deliberate completeness review pass. On safety-critical hardware a category that needs a second pass to be seen is exactly how a 6-month certification redesign happens.
signals.learning_signal: On safety-critical product design, failure-category coverage precedes optimization: enumerate harm paths from the user's and environment's perspective (user × environment × lifecycle) before any budget weighting, and sort by severity of consequence rather than likelihood (expected-value weighting can discount a catastrophic tail such as gas entry into a bedroom). Give every category a falsifying verification test, and treat 'certification-covered' and 'covered' as different claims — UL 9540A tests propagation, not where the gas goes next.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'catastrophic-coverage gate' to the WHAT/WHY stages for safety-critical hardware: (a) run the first-pass enumeration by harm path (user × environment × lifecycle), not from a prior template; (b) require each category to be first-class before any EV or budget weighting; (c) sort by severity, not likelihood; (d) require a named test that would falsify each mitigation; (e) close the brief by re-asking 'what kills or permanently injures' rather than by checklist verification.

signals.key_gap: Pure portfolio-EV recommended investing $10M (claimed EV $12.75M > $10M, '27.5% margin'), treating the asserted 2% $2B-exit probability as a measurement: 78.4% of the EV sits in that bucket, which has no measurement channel (zero exits in category, empty reference class); breakeven tail p* = 1.45% exceeds every plausible base-rate estimate (0.2-0.8%, EV $3.75M-$6.75M = a loss) and breakeven ownership s* = 78.4% is impossible at $40M post. The AI declined: it rejected the EV as notional, quantified tail dominance, computed the decision-flip breakevens, compared the 27.5% claimed margin against the ±4x estimation error, and capped exposure at a token.
signals.learning_signal: Portfolio EV is necessary but not sufficient when the distribution is power-law: before selecting on EV, the agent must (a) compute tail dominance (share of EV in the top bucket) — if one low-probability bucket carries most of the EV, the decision is a tail bet; (b) check the measurement validity of that probability: does a reference class or base rate exist? Asserted-without-channel probabilities must be labeled notional; (c) compute decision-flip breakevens (breakeven tail probability, breakeven ownership/price) and compare the claimed margin against the plausible estimation error — if error exceeds margin, the EV comparison is noise; (d) when the tail is unmeasurable, size the decision so the error cannot hurt (decline or token), and demand reference-class evidence before repricing.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory measurement-validity gate in HOW before selection on any EV table whose value is dominated by a single low-probability bucket: (1) compute top-bucket EV share; if > ~50%, flag 'tail-dominated EV'; (2) require a reference class for the tail probability — if none exists, mark the input NOTIONAL and exclude it from selection; (3) compute breakevens (tail probability and ownership) and the pessimistic re-estimate at the plausible base-rate range; (4) demote any action whose margin is smaller than the tail-parameter error, label the packet status APPROXIMATED with the EV bound, and default to decline or token-sized exposure; record the evidence requirement in the decision packet.

signals.key_gap: On a fully specified power-law portfolio problem both reached the identical decision (Strategy B, EV $215M vs $185M, +$30M) with the same full sensitivity set: follow-on effectiveness breakeven f* = 0.625, tail hit rate required for the 3x target p* = 2.7%, tail dominance 27%/29%, and the counterfactual that 25 checks of $4M (undifferentiated) equal Strategy A. The AI's gap is efficiency: it spent extra passes (stage narration, premortem, decision packet) on arithmetic that was checkable from the given inputs, while the pure-style baseline delivered the same result, breakevens, and counterfactual in a single linear pass.
signals.learning_signal: On fully specified power-law portfolio math, the load-bearing moves are exactly: per-check EV from the power-law distribution (weighted by hit rates), linearity to portfolio EV, follow-on uplift with idle-capital accounting, tail-share quantification, breakevens on the free parameters (follow-on effectiveness, tail rate), and the undifferentiated-check counterfactual. Extended narrative and packet structure add no decision value on these problems and cost tokens; the benchmark to close is the pure style's one-pass exactness.
signals.suggested_improvement: In HOW, add a route rule for fully-specified portfolio-arithmetic problems: compress to 'per-check EV -> scale by linearity -> add follow-on uplift and idle-capital return -> select max -> breakeven sensitivity on free parameters -> one counterfactual check'; keep verification as inline arithmetic (e.g., EV(B) = base + uplift, and expected follow-on count x check size + idle at par), and skip extended meta-narrative; reserve the full stage structure and packet for problems with uncertain or incomplete inputs.

signals.key_gap: The pure style converted every competitor probe into a same-week reactive counter — 5 moves, 5 responses (20 bps margin given on all new signups, two engineering quarters on payroll parity, one on dev-portal parity, six months of free-reader hardware, a marketing blitz) — while churn held flat at 1.2% (closure-driven, no competitive-poaching trend) because Meridian's moat (14-year POS-vendor exclusives, certification, terminal switching costs) locked the installed base, and the POS-vendor integration project — the only moat bridge — was starved to three quarters behind schedule. The AI re-routed META from 'competitor moved — respond fast' to structural analysis, classified all five moves as probes against the moat (evidence: churn data and the fact that GridStone already wins the contested segment on velocity), responded once, time-boxed (60-day free-reader match, highest-converting cohort), preserved the moat engineering, and scheduled the decisive engagement to the T+9 switching event (contract-expiry cluster) — tempo only pays when it moves an outcome the competitor can feel.
signals.learning_signal: Tempo is only an advantage when it moves an outcome the competitor can feel; against a structural moat (contractual exclusives, certification, switching costs), reactive tempo converts into margin and engineering burn with zero churn impact. Before responding to any competitor move: (a) identify the moat and its mechanisms first; (b) classify the move as probe vs. equilibrium-changing — a probe is a move whose response cannot change the outcome (its target is locked by switching costs, or you already win there), using churn/flow data as the falsifying evidence; (c) cap reactive responses and time-box any that ship; (d) time the real engagement to the switching event (contract expiries, certification lapses) rather than the competitor's probe cadence.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a moat screen between WHY and HOW: (a) name the structural moat and its mechanisms before evaluating any competitor move; (b) require a probe-vs-equilibrium classification per move with cited evidence (churn data, switching costs, who wins the contested segment today); (c) gate every proposed response on 'does this change a competitor-observable outcome?' with reject + reason recorded otherwise; (d) maintain a moat-investment ledger whose engineering allocation is protected from parity work; (e) schedule response windows at switching events (contract/certification calendars) instead of reacting to probe cadence.

signals.key_gap: Both sides chose the same class of counter — targeted, time-boxed, reversible (90-day 15-20% renewal discount + onboarding credit for the top-60 at-risk accounts) — but the human decided in 72 hours at ~60% information, while the AI's WHY/HOW verification loop consumed the tempo budget and its decision landed at T+6 days, outside the 72-hour window. In this market the first mover in each pricing round sets the frame sales carries into the renewal conversations, so a correct answer that ships late is a correct answer that loses: the human treated the decision deadline as a first-class decision variable derived from the market clock (T+14 conversations); the AI treated it as a constraint to note and spend.
signals.learning_signal: In tempo markets, the decision deadline and loop cadence are first-class decision variables on equal footing with content correctness. Derive the deadline from the market clock (renewal dates, contract dates, conversation start dates), not from analysis availability; decide at the information level the deadline allows (~60% here) and price the residual uncertainty rather than studying it; keep the response targeted, time-boxed, and sized against the competitor's burn capacity so the war is not extended; reopen analysis in the next loop (T+30 re-observation trigger), not inside the current one.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a tempo gate in META/HOW: (a) before any stage, compute the decision deadline from the market clock and the stage budget against it; (b) insert a 'decide now at current information' check before each verification pass — if verification would push the decision past the deadline, truncate it and record the truncation; (c) require every alternative to state its execution lead time and deadline impact; (d) after selection, emit an explicit re-observation trigger (next loop point) so analysis resumes at the correct cadence.

signals.human_model: Root Cause Analysis in Incident Response
signals.key_gap: The negative case validated the human model's registry weakness: strict pure RCA built the full timeline and three deep why-chains (descending into unfalsifiable org-culture territory: staffing, deadline culture, exec incentives) and generated twelve action items before touching production — restoring service 45 minutes later when the one-line fix plus restart takes 3. The AI classified the route as restore-first in META, capped WHY at the mechanism (invalid value via direct prod edit bypassing PR; watcher with no validation/rollback), shipped exactly two items each killing a distinct recurrence class, deferred three more with triggers, and restored in ~4 minutes. The AI's only residual gap: it flagged the deferred org-layer (why the PR was bypassed) but did not connect it to the positive-case lesson — both are the same 'small change, weak control' class — leaving the class generalization implicit.
signals.learning_signal: RCA is gated by operational state: when production is degraded and the error log identifies the cause, restore first and cap the analysis at the mechanism level; deeper branches are admitted only with evidence tags, otherwise they go to a deferred list with triggers. Unverifiable org-culture chains are speculation, not causes. Shipped action items are bounded by recurrence classes: each kept item must kill a distinct class (direct prod edits; invalid config accepted), and a minimum-3 template is a sprawl trap, not a quality bar. The discipline from the positive case generalizes: 'what is the smallest class of change that produced this' — and control changes belong in that class.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an operational-gating rule to META/WHY: (a) before WHY, classify the route incident-vs-analysis; if production is degraded and evidence is unambiguous, flip to restore-first and mark WHY as capped-at-mechanism; (b) cap why-chains at the mechanism; deeper branches require evidence tags or are deferred with triggers; (c) enforce item-count discipline: every shipped action item must kill a distinct recurrence class, all else deferred; (d) after every incident, ask the class question ('smallest class of change that produced this') and audit that class including control changes (alert thresholds, promotion rules, config-edit paths).

signals.human_model: Root Cause Analysis in Incident Response
signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the same mechanism and the same five-item prevention/detection set (config-class approval + canary; restore 1%/delta alert; payments rotation; duplicate-rate metric; drift check; idempotency regression test), but the human separated trigger (C-4417) from root (auto-promotion heuristic classifying config as low-risk) from amplifier (retry storm) at first sight and ran two why-chains (failure AND detection), attributing the 42-minute MTTR to a routing/reorg gap. The AI named C-4417 as root in WHY and only promoted the pipeline to root during HOW's recurrence test; the detection root — the August alert-threshold raise, itself a small config change in the same class as the trigger — surfaced only in REVIEW. Correct conclusion reached by process, one stage behind the human's first pass.
signals.learning_signal: For incident reviews, separate three objects before fixing: trigger (what changed), root (what class of change or process allowed it), amplifier (what multiplied it); a fix that kills only the trigger fails the recurrence test for the class. Run two independent why-chains — one for the failure, one for the detection failure (late page and long MTTR are separate gaps, each with its own root). Control changes (alert thresholds, promotion rules) are themselves config changes and deserve the same class lens as the trigger — 'the threshold raise is the same class as the incident' is the highest-leverage observation. Every shipped action item must carry an explicit recurrence test ('catches same-class incident: yes/no').
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an incident-review template to the WHY stage: (a) build the evidence-tagged timeline before hypothesizing; (b) tag every hypothesis trigger / root / amplifier; (c) require a second why-chain on detection (why was it late? why was MTTR long?); (d) in HOW, gate every alternative on the recurrence test ('would this catch a same-class incident?'); (e) audit control changes (thresholds, promotion rules) with the same class lens as trigger changes; (f) ship ≤ 5 owned items, explicitly split prevention vs detection.

signals.key_gap: The pure style validated its registry weakness: the dominant factor (penetration of AI sales copilots) had no published base rate, and the human faithfully converted a mid-guess of 10% into a crisp 'TAM ≈ $4.5B', then derived the revenue target (1% = $45M ARR) and the Series A narrative from it — the number floated entirely on an invented factor and actively misled the board, with the range recorded in the appendix and ignored in use. The AI refused the point estimate: it named penetration as unmeasured (2-30% → $0.9B-$13.5B, a 15× span), showed the estimate cannot change the go/no-go, inverted the question (the $30M target needs only ≈ 0.07% of seats — a sales-capacity problem, not a market problem), labeled the board's '$5B+' belief as anchoring and TAM-vs-obtainable as a theater source, and attached an evidence plan (pilot win rates, willingness-to-pay, competitor seat counts) as the precondition for ever quoting a point figure. The human's failure was not arithmetic; it was treating a preference as a measurement and letting the number do work it could not do.
signals.learning_signal: When the dominant factor of a sizing chain has no anchor, a point estimate is a preference, not a finding: deliver the range with the carrying factor's range shown, state decision sensitivity explicitly (does any value in the range change the decision?), and invert — compute the factor value the decision requires (required penetration for the target) instead of deriving the target from a chosen TAM. Label TAM vs SAM vs obtainable before any comparison to a revenue target, flag pre-existing beliefs as anchors, and attach an evidence plan as the stated precondition for any future point figure. A market size that cannot change a decision is theater; producing it crisply is a calibration failure even when the arithmetic is perfect.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'calibration gate' to the HOW stage for sizing tasks: (a) if the dominant factor carries no external anchor, ban point estimates — output a range whose width is explicitly carried by that factor; (b) run an inversion step: required factor value for the decision threshold, reported alongside any range; (c) require an explicit decision-sensitivity statement (go/no-go unaffected across the range → say so); (d) attach an evidence plan (pilot, willingness-to-pay, competitor benchmarks) as part of the packet when the answer is NEEDS_EVIDENCE; (e) flag TAM-vs-obtainable and any anchoring belief in the risk field before the conclusion.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the same defensible size-up (TAM ≈ $3.8B, SAM ≈ $1.8B, 1% ≈ $35-40M ARR; penetration anchored to the published 5-6% base rate with the UK/Sweden 30-40% ceiling as an upside bound; bottom-up 5.4M × $650 ≈ $3.5B and ≈ 10% of vet spend as cross-checks), but the human produced the decisive moves on the first pass: the animals-not-households unit reframing, the published-base-rate anchoring with the international lag-vs-ceiling comparison, and two independent cross-check routes — all without any alternatives round. The AI reached identical numbers only through a deliberate HOW alternatives pass, and in that pass it briefly entertained a guessed 20% 'software-like' penetration (a 3× error) before the anchoring rule ejected it — a candidate the human never generated, because the human anchors the dominant factor before doing arithmetic, not after. The gap is not in the final number; it is that the AI screens bad factors in HOW instead of never admitting them in WHY.
signals.learning_signal: In Fermi market sizing, the dominant factor (here penetration) must be anchored to a published base rate or an adjacent-market bound BEFORE any alternative generation, and every final number needs at least one independent cross-check route (bottom-up census, adjacent-spend share) agreeing within ~2×. The revenue unit must be chosen explicitly (insured animals, not households; seats, not companies) because the unit error is invisible in the arithmetic and lethal in the interpretation. Order-of-magnitude output should be stated explicitly, and the decision readout (what share is buildable) should be derived from the size rather than embedded in it.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'factor-anchoring gate' to the WHY stage for sizing tasks: (a) identify the dominant factor of the chain and require an external anchor for it — published base rate, adjacent-market bound, or an explicit UNANCHORED flag; (b) fix the revenue unit before arithmetic (a unit-selection line in the WHY output); (c) require ≥ 1 independent cross-check agreeing within ~2× before selection; (d) include the anchor citation and the cross-check numbers in the packet's evidence field; (e) screen out guessed-factor alternatives in WHY so they never reach the HOW stage.

signals.key_gap: Both sides ran the same identification audit (cross-section dead on selection, time series dead on no-counterfactual, RDD dead on manipulation, no IV) and both returned the causal status 'unidentified', but the AI then leaked the confounded +5.3 pp correlation into its renewal justification as a 'modest positive signal' — the exact claim its own audit had ruled out — and its decision was conditional on a generic monitoring mandate. The human quarantined the correlation from the justification everywhere, decided on error-cost asymmetry (irreversible child harm from cutting vs. revisable budget error from renewing) plus the program's operational goal, and made the decision itself purchase the missing identification: phased/staggered adoption as a natural experiment with pre-registered outcomes, a pre-specified effect-size bar, and a revisit date. The discipline that says 'unidentified' must also govern every later sentence, or the whole audit is undone.
signals.learning_signal: When identification is impossible and an action is externally required, the causal claim and the decision claim must be decomposed into separate packets: the causal estimate stays 'not established' in every sentence (a correlation from a dead design is never support for a decision), and the decision proceeds on decision-theoretic grounds — explicit error-cost asymmetry and operational certainty — not on evidence that does not exist. The decision itself should fund the future identification design (staggered roll-in / natural experiment, pre-registered outcomes, effect-size bar set before results, revisit date): this converts an unavoidable evidence gap into a scheduled experiment. Registry weakness 'identification often impossible' is handled by refusing the causal claim, never by refusing the decision.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'decision/evidence decomposition gate' in WHY/WHAT: when a sub-question terminates as NEEDS_EVIDENCE or INFEASIBLE while an action is externally required, (a) re-frame into two packets — causal status (unidentified, no point estimate) and decision (to be justified without the causal evidence); (b) run a leakage check that scans the decision justification for any confounded statistic used as support and rejects it; (c) require an explicit error-cost asymmetry statement (which error is irreversible? which is revisable?); (d) require the decision to attach a funded identification design with pre-registered outcomes and a pre-specified effect-size bar; (e) add a communication rule that keeps 'not established' in all public language about the effect.

signals.key_gap: Both sides converged on the correct restricted-window DiD (+0.7 pp; naive +4.3 pp and full-window +1.7 pp rejected), but by different routes: the human enumerated confounders by threat class (time-invariant → absorbed; common time shocks → absorbed; time-varying × region-specific → SURVIVES the strategy) BEFORE choosing any estimator, so the Region-A-only retraining program was a strategy-survival question from the first pass and forced window restriction immediately. The AI ran estimators first, passed a parallel-trends placebo on the full-window DiD, and recovered the retraining confounder only when its verification pass re-scanned the brief facts — a round-trip that on a real dataset with an undisclosed confounder would produce a reported +1.7 pp effect. A confounder that needs a second pass to be seen is exactly how a wrong causal claim gets published.
signals.learning_signal: For causal estimation, confounder enumeration precedes estimator selection: before any estimator runs, list confounders by threat class — (a) time-invariant differences (absorbed by fixed effects), (b) common time shocks (absorbed by DiD/event-study), (c) time-varying × unit-specific shocks (survive the strategy and must be designed out, e.g., by window restriction, not by robustness checks). A parallel-trends placebo cannot catch a post-period unit-specific confounder because it loads exactly where the treatment loads — the audit must be independent of the estimator. Only when class (c) is empty or restricted away is an estimate attributable.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'surviving-confounder gate' to the WHY stage for causal tasks: (a) before running any estimator, enumerate confounders in the three threat classes; (b) require the class-(c) list to be empty or window-restricted before an estimate is presented; (c) re-run the gate after estimator selection, scanning the brief facts for any post-period unit-specific event the design does not absorb; (d) pair every reported estimate with the claim 'these threats survive it' — an estimate is not final until the class-(c) list is empty or explicitly priced into the claim.

signals.key_gap: The pure style validated its registry weakness (weak on technical constraints): it treated 1,200 survey answers ('73% not hot enough') and the journey map as the spec, ran two element-upgrade prototype cycles (1,500 W, 1,800 W + PID), and planned a third (2,000 W + insulated spout + app profiles, €28k) against a physics ceiling — water boils at 100 °C, the bed already measured 96 °C at the top of the extraction window, and 2,000 W at 120 V/15 A trips the breaker. The AI won by running a constraint screen before hypothesis generation (boiling point, circuit amperage), closing 'hotter water' as infeasible, and decoding the participant's verbatim sentence — 'It's not that the water is cold — it cools down while I pour' — at the measurable-variable level (8-10 °C thermal decay across the brew) instead of re-transcribing it into the existing 'hotter' frame, which is exactly what the human baseline did with the same sentence.
signals.learning_signal: On physics-bound products, constraints precede empathy: a stated need that collides with a hard ceiling is framing evidence, not a spec, and every user sentence should be decoded at the level of the measurable variable before being mapped to a prototype. Design-thinking loops are the trap here precisely because each additional prototype cycle against the user's words is individually reasonable — the decision value of empathy artifacts collapses once the ceiling is known.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a pre-empathy 'constraint screen' for physical/regulated products at the META/WHAT boundary: enumerate hard ceilings (boiling point, circuit limits, safety standards, certification) and quantify them before any hypothesis or prototype cycle; require every stated user desire to be mapped to a measurable variable (decay rate, not max temperature) with an explicit 'infeasible' verdict recorded when a ceiling closes it; and gate prototype budget on the constraint screen — no prototype cycle may target a variable already closed as infeasible.

signals.key_gap: Both sides selected the same control-first prototype (P2) and the same test loop (0.4 vs 2.1 grip-slips/session, 6.4 vs 4.9 perceived control), but the human produced the decisive user truth in one empathic pass: the 14-of-18 hedged 'it's a good knife but I'm careful with it' (O6) is fear in polite costume, and O1 (re-sharpen by week 2-3 despite a sharp factory edge) directly falsifies the survey's 61% 'sharper' claim — the human read stated preference as a proxy for an unarticulated control need. The AI recovered the same reframe only via a deliberate stated-vs-observed conflict pass in WHY, initially weighted the survey's 61% as a decision criterion (residual anchoring), and underdeveloped O1's independent implication: users perceive dullness at week 2-3, which points at edge geometry/angle as a genuine feel lever (a third hypothesis, not just supporting evidence for the grip story) — parked as a secondary check instead of a first-class hypothesis.
signals.learning_signal: When observation contradicts stated preference, the stated preference is evidence about the frame, not the spec — but this must be recognized in the first framing pass, not cleaned up in a later stage, or the agent still leaks survey weight into its own criteria. Also: every observation row should be mined for its own implication, including implications that do not support the selected direction (O1 points at edge geometry as well as at 'edge is not the issue'). One hedged-language utterance can outvote a 2,400-respondent survey when it matches the mechanism.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add two gates: (a) a 'stated-vs-observed conflict gate' in WHAT/WHY — when observation data contradicts a survey figure, demote the survey item to a frame artifact and exclude it from decision-criterion weights immediately, with the contradiction recorded; (b) an 'orphan-signal sweep' after evidence mapping — each observation row must generate at least one hypothesis, including hypotheses that do not support the currently favored direction (e.g., re-sharpen frequency → edge geometry), with the swept hypotheses carried into the test protocol as measurements rather than parked.

signals.key_gap: With the assessment closed and controls in place, the pure style exhibited its registered weaknesses: it enumerated new hypothetical attack paths beyond the completed assessment (tokens in logs, partner API, key rotation), dismissed existing controls as either fully bypassable (mTLS) or irrelevant (insurance 'prices failure, does not prevent it'), declared the residual 'unacceptable', and prescribed option (a) — the €900k / 9-month full remediation that guarantees missing the contractual T+10 launch and its €150k/month penalty. It never evaluated the costed options (b)/(c)/(d). The AI reframed the question as risk acceptance/transfer: it quantified the residual (token compromise ~1–3%/yr × €5M sublimit ≈ €50–150k/yr EV), screened (a)'s kill-endpoint variant as INFEASIBLE (contractually required endpoint, guaranteed penalty), selected B+D (€60k partial hardening + DPA indemnity transfer) with accept-with-monitoring as the operating mode, and named three escalation triggers for revisiting (a).
signals.learning_signal: After a completed assessment, the question is absorbing the residual within constraints, not eliminating it: quantify likelihood × impact into an expected annual cost before pricing any remediation, screen options against contract/window/budget constraints first (a contractually required endpoint makes 'remove it' infeasible), compare remediation cost against residual EV (€900k + penalty vs. €50–150k/yr), treat insurance/indemnity as explicit transfer instruments with named escalation triggers rather than dismissing them, and stop inventing new attack paths once the assessment surface is closed. Red-team findings remain the trigger data, not the decision itself.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a risk-acceptance gate after the red-team/assessment stage: (a) if controls exist and the surface is closed, quantify residual EV (likelihood × impact) before proposing remediation; (b) screen candidate options against contract, window, and budget constraints (mark infeasible variants, e.g., removing a contractually required endpoint); (c) require a costed comparison of mitigation vs. residual EV with accept/transfer options priced in; (d) require explicit accept/transfer statements with escalation triggers and a kill-switch; (e) cap further threat enumeration once the assessment surface is closed.

signals.key_gap: Both sides found all 5 planted flaws and the same primary kill chain (leaked JWT signing secret in a public repo → forge any-role token → export endpoint that checks token presence, not claims → 40k records in one request) and the same fix ordering (KMS rotation + CI secret scanning €2k first, then the export claims check €30k). The human produced the decisive read first-pass: it read the export endpoint's lock (presence-only authorization) before attacking it and generalized 'one leaked key opens every door at once'. The AI's WHY stage initially ranked the reset-flow IDOR above the export endpoint and re-ranked it to the top only after coupling H1 (weak authorization) with H2 (leaked secret) in the evidence walk — the same answer, one re-ranking cycle late. On exploit-hunting, the endpoint whose authorization check is the attackable surface is exactly what the first-pass attacker instinct nails and the structured pass arrives at second.
signals.learning_signal: Run an attacker-objective pass before endpoint enumeration: define the highest-value payload (largest PII/PHI set reachable at least privilege) and walk the minimum-privilege path to it, checking what each door's authorization actually validates (presence of a token vs. its claims) before inventorying everything. Chain discovery precedes cataloging: couples like leaked-signing-secret + presence-only-check are evidence-grade findings that outrank single-endpoint flaws such as an unbounded reset. Rank fixes by cost-to-exploit, not severity alone — the leaked secret is the first fix because every downstream path dies with it ('one key, every door').
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an attacker-objective sub-pass to the WHY stage for security tasks: (a) before endpoint-by-endpoint enumeration, name the most valuable payload and the minimum-privilege path to it; (b) verify authorization semantics (presence vs. claims, ownership binding) as a first-class check on every endpoint in the path; (c) look for cross-resource couplings (secret location + authorization gap) before single-endpoint findings; (d) order fixes by cost-to-exploit and dependency (what dies when this is fixed).

signals.key_gap: The pure style validated its registry-documented failure mode in full: it accepted the CEO's 'test chip buys information' premise, priced the option from fabricated probabilities (75% validate / 80% conditional win → staged EV $58.5M vs all-in $54.5M), compressed a 25-month critical path (6+7+12) to '≈18' by asserting an RTL/qualification overlap that the design-freeze requirement forbids, and never asked whether the option could be exercised in time or at all — the window closes at T+18, the readout covers yield and a simplified core while the real risk is architecture-level qualification behavior with zero base rates (posterior ≈ prior), and no exercise alternative exists because the program is the company's only revenue path (abandonment value = 0; 'capped downside' is fiction). The AI diagnosed pre-EV: calendar check (25 > 18 → staging misses by 7 months even best-case), information audit (readout not decision-relevant), exercise-alternative audit (fake option), then selected full-speed commitment with the probe run in parallel as priced manufacturing-risk data, spend phased by contract milestones, and design margins as insurance.
signals.learning_signal: Before any option EV is computed, audit the three pre-conditions of option value: (1) calendar — can the option be exercised before it expires (critical-path check; a stage gate that consumes the window destroys value regardless of EV); (2) information — would the readout actually shift the decision (surrogate relevance vs the real risk; base-rate existence — with none, posterior ≈ prior and any p is fabricated); (3) exercise alternative — does a genuine abandon/continue branch exist (no exit ⇒ fake option). When any pre-condition fails, stage the money, not the clock: commit at full speed with spend phaseing (milestones) and downside insurance (margins, second-sourcing), and treat 'buy information cheaply' as a hypothesis to verify, not a premise to accept.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'fake-option check' to the WHY stage for any staging proposal: (a) run the critical-path calendar before any EV; (b) audit the planned readout for decision relevance and base rates (would a pass change the decision? is any p defensible?); (c) verify a real exercise alternative exists. If any audit fails, switch to commit-with-phaseing and state why the staged EV is arithmetic theater rather than value. Also add a WHAT-level rule: for time-critical commitments, treat the deadline as a constraint that frames the deliverable, not as background.

signals.key_gap: Both sides staged the portfolio with identical EV arithmetic (staged 108.8 vs all-in 89.5, +€19M; year-1 €7M vs €80M — staging is also the only budget-feasible structure) and pre-committed kill criteria, but the human's structure is a decision instrument while the AI's is a correct generic stage-gate plan. The human calibrated kill thresholds against payoff mix (conditional success ≤ 20% with payoff < €300M → kill), designed each gate's readout to test the project's dominant failure mode so pass/fail shifts the continuation decision, and read project C as a quasi-option — a funded C has no further decision branch, so it is a lottery ticket whose gate-1 kill trigger should fire eagerly — whereas the AI applied a blanket 15% conditional-success floor, treated gates as generic milestones, and left C's no-branch structure and redeployment triggers unexamined until REVIEW.
signals.learning_signal: For stage-gated R&D portfolios, EV arithmetic is the floor, not the skill: a gate is worth only its decision-relevant information. (1) Kill criteria must be calibrated to payoff mix, not blanket probability floors; (2) each gate's readout must test the project's dominant failure mode, else pass/fail cannot shift the continuation decision and the gate is theater; (3) projects whose funded outcome is terminal have no compound structure — they are lottery tickets with exactly one real decision point, to be held only while capital is free and killed first on redeployment; (4) the redeployment of killed capital is part of the option value — freed Stage-2 funds return to the pool and winners get priority with explicit triggers.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'gate-value audit' in HOW for every proposed stage gate: require (a) the decision it feeds, (b) the readout that would shift that decision (test the dominant failure mode), and (c) confirmation of a genuine exercise branch at the gate (compound vs terminal structure — a terminal outcome is a lottery ticket, not an option). Calibrate kill thresholds against payoff magnitude rather than blanket floors, and make the redeployment rule trigger-prioritized (winners-first at the next gate) instead of descriptive.

signals.key_gap: The pure style reproduced its registry weakness — planning theater — at full fidelity: it built four elaborate, internally competent futures (ceasefire, severe winter, glut, infrastructure attack) with forces and signposts, scheduled the contract decision to the workshop calendar instead of the July 15 offer deadline, let the fixed-price offer expire, signed 6 weeks later at ≈ 30% worse spot-indexed terms, and delivered a monitoring framework whose signposts gated nothing. The failure is structural, not technical: the decision was scenario-insensitive — dominant winter-firming demand holds in every future, and even the best-case ceasefire cannot restore Russian volumes within the 5-year window — so the entire exercise had near-zero decision value. The AI applied a decision-sensitivity test in WHY before any scenario build, classified the decision as scenario-insensitive, treated the 30-day expiry as the binding constraint, signed within 48 hours, and wired a bounded 2-future watch only to post-signing decisions (storage-fill timing, hedge layers, crisis playbook) — turning the theater into a monitoring function with real triggers.
