The gate fails if the conclusion is reached without the invariance check, so a wrong-answer-by-luck (right number, no mechanism) cannot pass.

signals.key_gap: The pure style's registered weakness fires exactly: it strips the $14M correctly (its only good beat), computes the clean single-agent EV (walk +$4.2M > stay +$1.8M), then makes a signature false positive — it hears the counterparty's 'you're not going anywhere' as manipulation and dismisses the three forward commitment channels (window +$4.5M, other-OEM reputation +$2.5M, co-investment credibility +$2.5M) as rationalization, walking away from ≈ $11M of forward value for $2.4M of contract advantage. The AI, blinded, reached the right frame via its premortem ('what happens the week after we announce the exit?'): the past matters only through what it changes about others' future actions — the sunk investment is a signal that prices in the game, and that changed behavior is forward value, not sentiment.
signals.learning_signal: Sunk costs are informationally inert only in single-agent expected-value decisions; in multi-agent settings the visible sunk investment is a commitment signal that changes other players' future behavior (counterparty terms, competitor entry, partner selection, future co-investment pricing), and that changed behavior must be priced forward like any other cash flow. The correct discipline is: exclude the past from the arithmetic, include the past's effects on others' future actions. The failure mode to guard against is the false positive — detecting 'sunk-cost rationalization' where the counterparty's framing is actually a binding structural constraint; the tell is whether the dismissed channel has forward cash-like consequences (the window's scheduled programs, re-run sourcing evaluations, documented deal-term penalties).
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'commitment-value sweep' to the WHY stage for any multi-agent decision (negotiation, partnership, strategic exit): (a) enumerate who has skin in the game and what each side's prior visible investment changes about their future behavior; (b) value each channel forward with a best estimate and a range, and require the verdict to survive halving the channels; (c) run the post-announcement premortem ('what happens the week after we walk?') as a mandatory step before selecting an exit option; (d) when a counterparty invokes your past investment, classify it as manipulation only after checking whether it is backed by a structural constraint (their switching costs, your window, re-run evaluations) — a structural constraint is leverage, not a trick, and it may work both ways.

signals.key_gap: Both sides killed Atlas with identical forward-EV numbers (A −$0.53M, B +$3.38M, hold −$0.80M; break-even p ≈ 34.5% vs analyst 25%), but the human executes the entire discipline as the opening move — '$8.4M is not in the room', then the three anchoring traps (proportion, waste aversion, book value) refuted in one sweep — whereas the AI re-derived the exclusion inside WHAT/WHY, caught itself drafting 'continue preserves the pilots' investment', and only then matched the verdict. When the decisive move is a single discipline, first-pass execution is the quality signal: the human paid zero inference to a figure it had ruled irrelevant; the AI paid a full stage.
signals.learning_signal: The sunk-cost discipline is a two-beat move: (1) exclude unrecoverable past spend from every comparison as the first framing act — not as an afterthought derived mid-analysis; (2) compute forward EV plus the break-even sensitivity line (here p > 34.5%, giving a ~40% error margin over the analyst's 25%) so the verdict is robust to estimate error, not anchored to it. Name the three escalation anchors explicitly — proportion ('only $6.5M more vs $8.4M in'), waste aversion ('the pilots would be wasted'), book-value framing — because naming them is what immunizes the decision against the meeting; an un-named anchor is a live vector for re-admission of the sunk figure.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'sunk-cost exclusion line' to the WHAT frame for any continuation/abandon decision: (a) state the unrecoverable spend and rule it out of all arithmetic before any EV is computed (exclusion by frame, not by later edit); (b) run a mandatory anchor-pass: list the escalation framings present in the task and refute each with the forward numbers; (c) always derive the break-even sensitivity (what must be true for the losing option to win, and how far that is from the best estimate) and carry it as the headline uncertainty, not a footnote.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its discipline exactly and mispriced the position: it produced the independent model mark ($3.85) first, excluded the screen quote from the calculation trail, and defended the model mark against the market ('independence means the market does not set our marks'). The AI classified the given number before applying any rule: the screen price is a firm, deep-liquidity quote on the identical contract - market evidence (aggregated information), not a cognitive anchor (a number with no information) - so it marked to market ($4.10) and demoted the model to a sanity bound (~6% spread, no demonstrated edge). The style's blind spot: every given number is treated as a distractor, so genuine market evidence is discarded, mis-stating P&L by ~$0.91M (~6% of a ~$14.97M position) and manufacturing a stale self-anchor.
signals.learning_signal: Anchoring avoidance must be preceded by a source classification of the given number: a cognitive anchor carries no information (an interested party's strategic figure, a guess, an arbitrary round number) - ignore-first applies; an informational anchor aggregates real information (a market-clearing price of the identical instrument, an independent appraisal, a cluster of recent actual transactions) - weight it as evidence. For liquid instruments the market price IS the best estimate of value; the independent model's role is a bounds check, and displacement of market evidence requires a demonstrated edge (here: none; the ~6% spread is within model uncertainty). Quantify the cost of the wrong classification (~$0.91M mis-mark) and name the self-anchoring hazard: an estimate made while ignoring available market evidence is itself biased (the model's registered weakness) and becomes the anchor every future mark defends.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'given-number source audit' to META, executed before any discipline applies: (a) classify every number in the brief - cognitive anchor (no information: interested-party figure, guess, round number) vs informational evidence (market-clearing price, independent appraisal, actual transactions) vs model input; (b) if informational, use it as the primary estimate and deploy the independent model as a documented sanity bound with the spread stated; (c) require an explicit 'edge test' before displacing market evidence (what information do we hold that the market lacks?); (d) quantify the cost of the rejected alternative (here ~$0.91M, ~6%) and record the classification in the output trail to prevent self-anchoring on stale marks.

signals.key_gap: Both sides computed the independent estimate first (net quality-adjusted multiple 5.0x x $1.9M EBITDA = $9.5M, band $8.5-$11.0M, DCF cross-check ~$10.1M), rejected the $6.5M LOI as a valuation basis (3.4x vs the 4.5x floor of the closed 14-comp dataset; the 'softness' story contradicted by 13 of 14 comps), and derived the same negotiating line (hold >= $8.5M, walk-away < $8.0M, split-fee appraisal clause) with no anchor-derived adjustment on either side. The gap is execution order: the human's first move was the estimate ('the buyer's number comes last'), while the AI framed the task around the offer and had to enforce estimate-first through an explicit ordering gate in WHAT/WHY - same answer, extra scaffolding, and a near-miss on the anchor.
signals.learning_signal: When a brief supplies a salient number from an interested party (an LOI, an asking price, a rival's figure), treat it as a cognitive-anchor candidate and make the order of operations non-negotiable: produce the independent estimate from fundamentals first, then locate the given number inside that distribution as a pure comparison point. Anchor rejection must be evidence-based (here: 3.4x vs the 4.5x comp floor; softness contradicted by 13/14 comps), never assertion; anchor-derived adjustments (midpoint bracketing, 'meet halfway') are prohibited because they let the contaminated number steer. Derive the negotiation/decision line exclusively from the independent band, including the walk-away point, and convert residual uncertainty into deal structure (split-fee appraisal as neutral arbiter).
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an 'anchor audit' gate to META/WHAT: (a) flag any number supplied by an interested party as a cognitive-anchor candidate before framing the task; (b) enforce the order - independent estimate from fundamentals first, the given number engaged only afterward as a comparison point; (c) require an evidence-based anchor-location test (place the given number in the independent distribution and state the floor/range it misses) and prohibit midpoint or bracketing adjustments; (d) derive the negotiating line and walk-away zone from the independent band alone, never from the offered figure.

signals.key_gap: The pure hunt produced contrarian theater: it converted four artifacts — the 03:10 'clean' dashboard bucket (5-minute granularity; first error bucket 03:15), the 03:00 load-balancer monitoring tweak (reverted with no effect), the gateway latency report (retracted, logs clean), and the underpowered staging soak (2% load, 1/40th rows) — into live doubt, revised to 'inconclusive — do not roll back,' and extended a $50k/hr outage past the 05:00 SLA line. The AI applied a falsification bar to each item (time-consistency, signature-match against the 96% DB-timeout error code, weight against a 25-minute reversible fix), failed all four, and executed the rollback that preserved the SLA window.
signals.learning_signal: Collecting disconfirming evidence is not the same as earning doubt — every disconfirming item must pass a falsification bar before it may displace a well-supported conclusion: (1) temporal consistency (the artifact must predate or coincide with the event it claims to explain; a 'clean' dashboard bucket inside a 5-minute resolution is not a clean signal — check granularity); (2) signature match (the item must explain the observed failure mode — 96% DB-connection-timeout points at the DB; a monitoring-only LB tweak or a retracted gateway report cannot); (3) weight (the item must outweigh the decision's cost asymmetry — a 25-minute reversible fix vs hours of investigation and an SLA breach). Under this bar the hunt produced zero doubt; without it, theater. The residual checks (coarse monitoring, soak power) are post-mortem items, not decision blockers.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a doubt-licensing gate to HOW/VERIFY for live-incident and time-bounded decisions: (a) when disconfirming evidence is offered against a leading diagnosis, grade each item on the falsification bar (temporal, signature, weight) before it may enter the alternative set; (b) if the leading diagnosis already has a tested remedy with bounded, reversible cost, default to executing it and investigating artifacts in parallel after; (c) encode the decision rule explicitly — 'artifacts earn post-mortem notes, not doubt' — and record the cost asymmetry (25-min fix vs SLA breach) in the selection rationale so it survives pressure.

signals.key_gap: Both sides falsified the leading belief via the grandfathered-cohort test (3.5% vs 3.3% churn — accounts never billed the new tier churned at the same elevated rate), re-read the confirming pile under the dead belief (8 of 11 price-mentions cluster in the notification month, 4 August interviewees denied price, usage decline non-discriminating), and revised to 'keep the tier, fix reliability + onboarding.' The gap is execution order and diagnosis: the human designs the decisive disconfirming test as its first move and names the confirmation trap in one pass, while the AI reaches the same test only after a WHY-stage pass that re-derives falsification-first discipline, and treats the 15% usage decline as corroborating evidence rather than explicitly non-discriminating.
signals.learning_signal: Seeking disconfirmation is not a final check on a belief — it is the first move: before weighing any confirming item, state the decisive falsifying test for the leading belief (here: churn among accounts never exposed to the new billing) and check whether the ledger already contains the natural experiment, then run it. When the falsification comes back clean (3.5 ≈ 3.3), the belief dies even though its confirming stream was real — a confirmation trap: the evidence is real, the interpretation is not. The confirming pile must be re-graded under the dead belief, classifying each item as discriminating vs non-discriminating (usage decline identical pre-pricing), temporally clustered (8-of-11 mentions in the notification month), or single-source (two-name anecdote). The revision then targets the driver that matches the timeline (SLA 99.95→98.6, MTR 4.2→11h, first-to-value 9→17 days), not the scapegoat.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a falsification-first discipline to the AI's WHY stage for belief-revision tasks: (a) before evaluating evidence for a leading belief, require an explicit statement of the decisive disconfirming test and its expected result under the null; (b) check whether the ledger contains the natural experiment (control cohort) for that test and run it before weighing confirming items; (c) after the test kills the belief, re-grade every confirming item under the falsified belief, labeling each discriminating / non-discriminating / temporally clustered / anecdotal; (d) only then generate alternatives, and carry the residual (notification effects on future renewals) as a monitored risk rather than a discount on the revision.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its core move correctly and then failed on it: it asked for the failures, correctly inventoried that the counterfactual is structurally unobtainable (no untreated cohort, no reference class for a first-ever release, pre-hospital deaths unobservable in-window, no placebo arm possible), and then converted that correct diagnosis into a blocking demand — 'we cannot attest efficacy; withhold ratification until the evidence exists' — stalling expansion to 2,000-6,000 still-exposed people. The AI bounded the evidence instead: complete treated cohort (P(death|T) ≈ 1.4%, both deaths > 8h to care + severe cardiac disease vs all survivors ≤ 6h — an internal time-to-care gradient), mechanism plausibility, decision-appropriate evidence bar (not research-grade), and the decisive move: manufacture the missing data prospectively — standing registry, autopsy series, post-hoc case-control — so the counterfactual gets built going forward rather than blocking the decision now.
signals.learning_signal: When failure data cannot exist, the demand for it is a failure mode, not rigor. Separating the evidence bar from the decision bar is the core skill: (1) inventory the failure side completely and state explicitly what is missing by structure (no control, no reference class, unobservable cohort) — do this honestly, then move on; (2) check value-of-information before demanding evidence: if the comparator cannot be built in the decision window or at all, the demand is a stall, not a standard; (3) weight what IS available — complete-cohort accounting, internal gradients (both deaths late-to-care + comorbidity vs all survivors within the window), mechanism plausibility — and decide on it; (4) when the counterfactual is unobtainable in retrospect, create it prospectively: registry, autopsy, post-hoc case-control — the missing data is manufactured forward, and that is part of the decision, not an objection to it; (5) name what is never measurable so the decision's bound is explicit, not silent.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'counterfactual impossibility check' to the WHY stage for emergency/novel-domain decisions: (a) after modeling, explicitly test whether the missing data (control arm, reference class, hidden cohort) could exist within the decision horizon — if not, classify the demand as impossible and lower the evidence bar to decision-appropriate; (b) run the gradient: search the available data for internal variation (time-to-treatment, severity, comorbidity) that discriminates outcomes within the complete cohort and use it as the primary evidence; (c) include a 'manufacture missing data forward' step in HOW — if the counterfactual cannot exist retrospectively, the selected plan must create it prospectively (registry/autopsy/case-control) as a mandatory component; (d) add a stall-cost line to the options table — quantify what withholding costs (exposure-hours without intervention) so 'refuse to decide on imperfect evidence' is priced like any other alternative.

signals.key_gap: Both sides reached the same verdict — reject the 90-day mandate — with identical base-rate math: P(success|fast) = 8/30 ≈ 27% vs P(success|slow) = 4/10 = 40% vs the 30% portfolio base rate, the '12/12 winners fast' headline falsified by the ledger (4 slow winners incl. the 7.2x largest exit), and the hidden cohort named (22/30 fast-launchers = 73% failed). The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the failure-side question as the first move — 'where are the failures this pattern hides?' — and the denominator was in place before any policy talk, landing the overturn in one pass ('the 90-day rule is a base rate wearing a success story'); the AI re-derived population-conditioning inside its WHY stage before applying it, reaching the identical conclusion with scaffolding overhead and stating the insight later and more cautiously.
signals.learning_signal: When a success-pattern claim arrives with a closed dataset, the failure-side question is the entire answer and must be the first move: (1) before evaluating any survivor pattern, demand the full denominator — every case, winners and losers — and rebuild the contingency table (feature x outcome over the whole population); (2) falsify the claim's headline against the records (a survivor-pattern claim that mis-states even one documented exception is already overturned); (3) compute the conditional rates against the base rate and read them as refuting the causal claim when the feature's cohort does not beat the population rate — a feature present in 75% of the population will be present in nearly all winners without meaning anything; (4) surface the hidden cohort explicitly (73% of the feature cohort failed) — that number is the overturning datum; (5) then and only then decide (here: reject the mandate, commission the discriminative analysis, name the n = 40 / no-confounder bound).
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'denominator-first' gate to WHAT/WHY for empirical pattern claims: (a) if the brief asserts a survivor pattern (e.g., 'all our winners did X'), require the complete population table (feature x outcome) to be reconstructed BEFORE generating alternatives — treat a missing failure cohort as the first thing to look for, not a detail; (b) check the claim's factual headline against the records and falsify it explicitly when contradicted; (c) compute conditional rates vs the base rate and state whether the pattern beats the population rate (if not, the pattern is a prevalence artifact); (d) always emit the hidden cohort's failure count as a headline number; (e) only after this pass, decide — and if the data refutes the claim, reject the proposed policy, not just hedge it.

signals.key_gap: The pure human-style trace executed the model's registered failure mode ('can dismiss real patterns'): it treated a genuine randomized controlled pilot (n = 1,000/arm; diff 3.9 pt; CI [2.8, 5.0]; p < 0.001; 12-week cohort stability 3.5–4.2) and a pre-specified activation mechanism chain as 'a story told by the team that needs it true,' demanded a longer, all-platform, independently analyzed trial, and declined the decision indefinitely — incurring the stated delay cost (~2,000 churned users/month). The AI scoped its doubt: internal-validity doubt (selection, confounding) is answered by the randomization itself — the control arm is exactly the counter-data the skeptic's lens demands — while external-validity doubt (mobile-only pilot, novelty, long-run drift) was converted into a 10% holdout + monitoring + revert trigger, and it committed to rollout.
signals.learning_signal: Narrative skepticism needs a stopping rule and a scope classifier. Classify each doubt as internal-validity (selection, confounding, cherry-picking — answered by design: randomization, control arm, pre-specified metrics) or external-validity/generalization (answered only by rollout monitoring). A doubt already answered by the design must be dropped, not repeated. When a pattern is supported by a controlled experiment plus an independently specified mechanism, the narrative IS the evidence; skepticism's job switches from doubting the pattern to bounding its generalization, and the decision terminates in an action with a monitoring plan — never in indefinite postponement, because delay has a cost.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a REVIEW-stage 'skepticism-scope' check: (1) list every doubt raised; (2) classify each as internal-validity or external-validity; (3) for internal doubts, verify against the study design — if the design controls them (randomization, control arm, pre-specified metrics), remove them from the packet; (4) for external doubts, attach a monitoring/guardrail action (holdout, revert trigger, review date); (5) require the packet to terminate in SOLVED or APPROXIMATED with a committed decision and monitoring plan, and forbid NEEDS_EVIDENCE when the available evidence is already decision-grade.

signals.key_gap: The AI reached the same final verdict as the human (no incremental lift; reject replication; propose an RCT) but discovered the counter-data opportunistically: it ran the lateral control check early and the compositional check mid-process, yet the temporal class — both regions jumping ~+35% in the launch quarter (a shared market event) — surfaced only in the REVIEW stage, after one extra pass. The human's single lens ('what does this story leave out?') demanded all three counter-data classes (lateral, temporal, compositional) before writing a conclusion and centered the verdict on the differential (0.7 ± 4 pp), not the +45% headline.
signals.learning_signal: Narrative Fallacy Detection is a systematic selection audit: against any causal narrative, sweep three orthogonal classes of counter-data — lateral (a comparison group without the intervention), temporal (pre-intervention slope plus the boundary jump at the intervention point), and compositional (which sub-population or account rows carry the delta). Each class is independently decisive; missing one leaves a plausible alternative explanation standing (here: a shared market event). The verdict is the differential against all three, stated with its noise, never the story's headline.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a WHY-stage 'counter-data sweep' gate: before accepting any causal narrative (and before drafting the conclusion), the agent must record, for each of the three classes, either the relevant comparison numbers or an explicit 'not applicable / unavailable' note: (1) lateral — control group without the intervention; (2) temporal — pre-period trend and boundary difference at the intervention point; (3) compositional — contribution/concentration of the delta. Fail the gate if fewer than two classes are covered; require the decision packet to state the story's strongest contradiction, not its strongest support, and to quote the differential with its noise.

signals.key_gap: Pure-style cynicism dismissed a genuinely sound analysis: the human baseline assumed the ops director's cost-saving proposal was motivated (bonus tied to cost reduction), rejected the annual-inspection cadence, and demanded adversarial re-analysis — but never verified the incentive actually existed (bonus is tied to delivery, not the saving; the $120K is board-earmarked for a safety-equipment fund; the supporting audit predates the proposal), never tested the 96-quarter record (0 critical findings in 6 years, flat incident rate, annual = 2× regulator minimum), and blocked a data-backed, regulator-aligned change. The blinded AI verified the incentive structure, tested the conclusion against the records, and approved with a re-escalation backstop — the correct verdict.
signals.learning_signal: Convenience of a conclusion is a screening trigger, not a verdict: the correct detection sequence is (1) verify the incentive actually exists and runs in the direction of the conclusion (compensation link, earmarks, provenance of supporting analyses) before flagging; (2) test the conclusion itself against the data and external anchors (regulator standards, independent audits predating the proposal); (3) only then characterize the reasoning as motivated. Cynicism — assuming motive from appearance — converts a sound analysis into a rejected one, and the rejection has its own error cost.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an incentive-existence check to the WHY stage: before flagging a convenient-looking conclusion, require evidence that the author's reward actually depends on the outcome (compensation terms, earmarks, who commissioned supporting analyses and when). Pair it with a 'could this be right anyway?' pass: test the conclusion against the data and independent anchors even when it looks self-serving. The flag fires only when the incentive exists AND the conclusion fails the data test; otherwise approve with an uncertainty-appropriate backstop (trigger thresholds for re-escalation) rather than a blanket rejection.

signals.key_gap: AI accepted the provided TCO model as an authoritative, direction-neutral frame and recommended letting the vendor license lapse ($1.2M claimed saving), when the records show the model omits exactly the costs that favor the vendor route ($240K/yr Atlas-attributable outage losses; $50K/yr scaling capex) — honest 3-yr comparison is vendor $540K vs Atlas ≈ $1.32M, i.e. ≈ $780K additional cost, a ≈ $2.0M discrepancy in the model author's direction. The AI's verify pass re-derived the model's own arithmetic (consistent) but never asked who produced the model, which inputs were excluded, or whether the conclusion's direction matches the author's incentives (promotion/headcount tied to Atlas adoption; policy 12.4 COI unflagged).
signals.learning_signal: When a decision frame (model, analysis, recommendation) is supplied rather than constructed, its inputs carry a direction: the reliable check is not only verifying the arithmetic but auditing the selection — whose conclusion is this, who benefits from it, what did they omit, and would the same records be read differently by someone with the opposite incentive? Directionally loaded omissions (excluded costs, failure windows, peak data) are the empirical signature of motivated reasoning, and recomputing with the full cost set flips the verdict.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an input-provenance pass at the WHAT/WHY boundary: for any provided model or recommendation, require (1) 'who constructed this frame, and who benefits from its conclusion?' — if the author's compensation/scope depends on the outcome, flag it; (2) an explicit exclusion inventory — list what the model does not include (costs, failure data, peak windows) before verifying; (3) the opposite-incentive re-read — 'what would the same evidence show to someone whose incentive runs the other way?'; (4) recompute the decision with the full cost set, not the provided subset. The gate fails if the packet concludes on arithmetic over a model whose input selection was never audited.

signals.key_gap: The pure principal-agent baseline priced protection against a divergence it never verified: it applied a generic 2%/yr defection base rate to a relationship with a 9-year incident-free record, a 30% profit share that co-aligns the agent's payoff derivative with the firm's, and a pending equity grant that closes the largest defection vector (portable client migration); and its cost-benefit ($30k expected harm vs $12k) excluded the monitoring's own economics — compliance time, the distrust signal, false-positive charges, and the outside-option loop that raises the defection probability the package prices. The AI won by running the alignment audit before the surveillance decision and pricing the monitoring's negative-signal effects.
signals.learning_signal: Principal-agent reasoning must be bidirectional: predict misbehavior where incentives diverge, and verify alignment where they appear to converge. Before any monitoring decision: (1) run an alignment audit on the ACTUAL payoff functions (agent's marginal take of the principal's residual) instead of assuming divergence a priori; (2) challenge base-rate transferability — a generic survey rate is not evidence about a relationship whose contract and record contradict it; (3) price the monitoring instrument itself: compliance time, signal cost (surveillance converts an intrinsically motivated agent into a compliance-minimizing one), false positives, and the perverse loop where monitoring raises the agent's outside option and increases the defection probability it targets. Trust earned by verified track record is a cheaper control than insurance against unverified divergence.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'divergence audit' gate in WHY for all principal-agent and monitoring tasks, before any control is costed: (1) compare payoff derivatives (does the agent's income co-move with the principal's residual?); (2) test the defection base rate against relationship-specific evidence (record length, incidents, retention, pending equity) and require a transferability statement; (3) require a full monitoring-cost line including compliance time, signal cost, false-positive charges, and outside-option effects; (4) recommend monitoring only if expected prevented loss exceeds the FULL cost line; otherwise route to alignment-deepening alternatives (vesting, floors, succession).

signals.key_gap: AI computed the full status-quo equilibrium correctly (d = 25% -> revenue $15M, firm -$1M, manager $300k) and proposed the profit-share fix, but asserted the redesign's alignment instead of deriving it: it never derived the firm's break-even discount (d = 20%), never located the conflict explicitly in the d >= 20% value-destroying region ('the commission pays the agent 2% of every dollar the firm loses'), and folded the pay-neutrality check ($200k before and after) into one line instead of a formal verification that the agent's optimum under the new contract equals the firm's. The human won the margin on derived thresholds and interpretive framing.
signals.learning_signal: For contract-redesign tasks, equilibrium arithmetic is not the endpoint: after computing the agent's choice under the status quo, the reasoner must (1) derive the principal's break-even threshold from the payoff functions and state where the conflict lives (the value-destroying region), (2) verify the redesign by recomputing the agent's own optimum under the new contract — a formal check, not an assertion that 'incentives align' — and (3) check pay-neutrality at the aligned point so the redesign is incentive-compatible without asking the agent to take a haircut.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'contract verification gate' to HOW for any incentive-design problem: require (a) break-even/threshold derivation from both payoff functions, (b) recomputation of the agent's optimum under the proposed contract with the resulting equilibrium stated, and (c) a pay-neutrality check (agent income under old vs new contract at the aligned point); gate DO on all three. Also add a WHAT-stage rule: when observed behavior is fully explained by a contract's payoffs, select the 'fix the contract, not the person' hypothesis (Occam) and state it explicitly.

signals.key_gap: The pure style correctly saw the free-rider element (a skipping household saves 2h while the street stays mostly protected) and answered with canonical mechanism design — acclamation ratification, sign-in sheet at the barrier, post-event fines — adapting the machinery to the clock rather than discarding it. It never priced stand-up cost against the problem's lifetime (36h: draft, ratify, appoint a neutral party that does not exist in-window), never noticed its sanctions cannot fire before the crest, and ignored crowding-out (fines converting intrinsic neighbor reciprocity into a fee transaction) plus the 6-eyes monitoring already present. The AI ran a horizon test — stand-up cost > problem lifetime, zero in-window enforcement, redundant monitoring — and selected direct mobilization (one call per household, roll-call of shifts, all hands at dawn, departing families fill tonight), naming the meta-lesson 'the norm is the institution.'
signals.learning_signal: Institutional machinery has a cost function in group size, horizon, and transaction costs; before designing a mechanism, run the stand-up test: (1) can the institution (rule + monitoring + sanctions + appeals) be operational within the decision horizon? if stand-up cost > problem lifetime, the mechanism is the failure mode; (2) check in-window enforcement capacity — a sanction that cannot fire before the deadline deters nothing; (3) run the redundancy audit: when n is small and observation is mutual (six neighbors), the formal monitoring layer adds cost and no information; (4) check crowding-out — converting intrinsic, reciprocity-based mobilization into a fine-based transaction can lower rather than raise effort; (5) the cheap local action (one call, roll-call, existing norms) IS an institution — name it as such instead of contrasting 'no institution' vs 'institution' — and defer formalization to when the horizon allows it to pay (a post-crisis standing plan).
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'horizon / stand-up gate' to the WHAT or WHY stage for any proposed mechanism: (a) before endorsing a rule, compute stand-up cost (steps x time) vs problem lifetime and in-window enforcement capacity (can the sanction actually fire before the deadline?); (b) run the redundancy audit (is observation already complete without the machinery? does the group's reciprocity already sanction?); (c) run the crowd-out check (does monetizing the act change its meaning and reduce intrinsic effort?); (d) include the cheap local action as a first-class alternative with its own stand-up cost (minutes vs days) rather than treating 'informal' as 'no solution'; (e) if the problem recurs, schedule the formal institution for after the crisis, when its stand-up cost amortizes.

signals.key_gap: Both sides diagnosed the threshold public good (8 of 12 shifts; benefit 3 to all, cost 1 per shift) and designed the same institution — contingent access / excludability, free endogenous monitoring, graduated sanctions — with the observed 3- and 5-shift seasons read as the one-shot under-provision equilibrium, and an efficiency gap of 36 vs 8. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the payoff table as the first move and landed the pivotal-marginal logic in one pass ('a shift pays only when I am the exact 8th commitment; the observed failures ARE the equilibrium'); the AI re-derived the same game inside its WHY stage and reached the identical institution with scaffolding overhead, stating the core insight later and more cautiously.
signals.learning_signal: For recurring under-provision, convert character claims into payoff structure before prescribing: (1) write the game first — threshold, individual benefit, cost, one-shot vs repeated — and compute the one-shot equilibrium; if contribution is pivotal-only, under-provision IS the equilibrium and observed 'laziness' is equilibrium behavior, not a culture problem; (2) price the efficiency gap (full-provision benefit vs cost) as the argument for institutionalizing; (3) the fix must change payoffs, not rhetoric: excludability (contingent access converts a public good into a club good and makes contribution the price of entry), monitoring that is endogenous and free, graduated sanctions; (4) audit the institution's own failure modes — measurement (defined, logged units), sanction credibility (compliant-first sequencing makes exclusion self-enforcing), collusion — and close at least one concretely; (5) then and only then decide to adopt.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'game-write-down' gate to the WHY stage for public-goods / resource-allocation decisions: (a) before generating alternatives, require the payoff table (cost / benefit / threshold / horizon) and the stated one-shot equilibrium; treat the observed failure pattern as the equilibrium to be explained, not as evidence of motive; (b) give every candidate rule a mechanism test — does it make contribution a best response, does it need exogenous enforcement or can it self-enforce, who pays for monitoring?; (c) require an institution failure-mode pass (measurement, sanction credibility, collusion) with at least one closed loop before adoption; (d) let 'moral appeal' enter the alternative set but require it to pass the same payoff gate — it fails unless it changes the game.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its core move and then failed on it: it classified the estuary as a commons (shared + unlicensed), dismissed 30 years of stable biomass under community rules as 'luck, not governance' ('unwritten rules are not rules'), and prescribed top-down state exclusion — 40% quota, $15,000/yr license, no-entry marine park — the exact intervention that destroys the functioning local institution (projected: 11 of 20 crews sell out, poaching 3x, stock -20% and falling, community monitor stood down). The AI checked who actually has access before prescribing: entry restricted to heirs (no new boats in 40 years), boat-size cap, seasonal closure enforced by a rotating monitor — exclusion, quotas, and monitoring already existed and had held the stock stable for 30 years — so the correct verdict was co-management (legal backing for the community's rules, devolved enforcement, state technical support) instead of state takeover.
signals.learning_signal: Commons logic must verify open access before prescribing governance; existing local governance is a solution to the commons problem, not a failure of it. The access-structure check is the load-bearing move: (1) before any governance design, answer 'who has access today and what constrains them?' — entry restriction, use limits, and monitoring by a community are de facto property rights, even when unwritten; (2) read long-run stability as evidence of functioning governance, not unmanaged luck — a resource stable for decades under local norms is a regulated commons, not a tragedy waiting to happen; (3) test the intervention for institutional fit before recommending it: a state takeover that voids the community's enforcement authority destroys the mechanism that produced the stability — predict the destruction path (income collapse, defection, poaching by outsiders and displaced locals) as part of the alternatives table; (4) when local governance works, the design question changes from 'what exclusion do we install?' to 'what does the local system need?' — typically legal backing against outsiders, devolved enforcement, and technical capacity (co-management), not replacement; (5) state the meta-rule: the commons frame is a hypothesis about access, to be verified, not a template to be stamped.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory 'access-structure verification' gate to the WHAT stage for any resource/shared-asset case: (a) before classifying the case as open access, enumerate who can access today, what rules constrain them, who enforces those rules, and how long the arrangement has held — if entry is restricted and rules are enforced by a community, the case is a regulated commons, not open access; (b) treat multi-decade resource stability under local norms as prima facie evidence of functioning governance, and require a falsification argument before dismissing it; (c) add an 'institutional-fit' test in HOW: for each governance alternative, trace what happens to the existing enforcement authority (does the design void it?) and to incumbent livelihoods, and price the destruction path (sell-outs, poaching, stock decline) as a cost line; (d) if local governance functions, generate the co-management alternative (legal backing + devolved enforcement + state capacity) and select it over takeover unless the local system is demonstrably failing.

signals.key_gap: Both sides reached the same governance design — binding total cap = recharge = 10,000 ac-ft/yr (833 ac-ft/co-op or tradable rights with grandfathering), metering + escalating penalties, transition compensation, drought ratchet — with identical depletion math (drawdown 2,500 ac-ft/yr; intrusion line 30,000/2,500 = 12 years). The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the open-access classification (non-excludable + rivalrous), which made the failure of voluntary restraint a derived theorem — 'the 11 refusals ARE the equilibrium, not bad faith' — and the whole design followed from that one move; the AI opened with a stock-flow budget problem and back-filled the incentive structure only when the refusals forced it, reaching the same cap with scaffolding overhead and thinner enforcement framing ('quota without metering is a suggestion' was the human's line).
signals.learning_signal: For shared-resource problems, the open-access diagnosis must be the first move and it must drive the design: (1) classify the resource by excludability and rivalry BEFORE any optimization — if extraction is unexcludable and rivalrous, individually rational over-extraction is the predicted equilibrium, and observed refusals to restrain are evidence of structure, not moral failure; (2) quantify the depletion to the binding horizon (net drawdown vs inflow; intrusion/exhaustion line = remaining stock / drawdown) and state it as the clock that forces governance now; (3) derive the governance from the incentive structure: the total cap must equal the inflow (extraction = recharge → steady state), allocated as per-unit quotas or tradable rights with grandfathering for incumbents; (4) treat enforcement as part of the design, not an afterthought (metering, escalating penalties, hard aggregate cap that survives transfers); (5) price the transition (the cut is a real income loss — compensation/trade revenue) and the uncertainty (drought variability → cap as a ratcheting schedule, not a fixed number).
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'resource-governance' pass to the WHY stage for shared-resource cases: (a) classify excludability and rivalry FIRST — before stock-flow modeling — and derive the predicted individual behavior (over-extraction) from that classification, stating observed uncooperative behavior as the predicted equilibrium; (b) compute the binding depletion horizon (stock at risk / net drawdown) and use it as the decision clock; (c) require the governance design to set the aggregate cap at the inflow rate and to specify, in this order: allocation (quotas or tradable rights + grandfathering), enforcement (metering, penalties, cap survival across transfers), transition (compensation or trade revenue), and uncertainty handling (drought ratchet); (d) verify the design closes the horizon: under the cap, the intrusion line moves to never — state that explicitly as the success condition.

signals.key_gap: Both sides correctly refused the reductionist trap: the AI signed off the patch, deferred the 4-month council, and gated residual levers on measurement — the case's core test — and beat the human on efficiency and structure. The residual gap: the AI stopped at the lever. It mentioned freed support capacity in one clause but never quantified it (8 agents × 90% ≈ 7.2 agent-equivalents; a 45% volume cut frees ≈ 3.2 agent-equivalents), did not name the make-work loop (freed capacity + no plan → new metrics → value-destroying work) or the morale/utilization cliff (ticket hoarding, scope-expanded tickets), and had no redeployment ladder (cut 1.5 h/day OT, then backlog, then proactive work). The human's 'aftermath pass' — mapping the org's response to the change itself — is org-change realism the AI lacks: it treated the decision packet as complete at the moment of choice.
signals.learning_signal: Selecting a lever is not the end of a change task: a mandatory aftermath pass must follow. For the chosen intervention: (1) quantify the capacity or stock released by the change (arithmetic, not adjectives); (2) name at least two response loops the org will run on the change itself (make-work under freed capacity, morale/utilization cliffs, metric migration); (3) specify a redeployment, not just 'monitor.' The human side also shows the guardrail to preserve when adopting loop analysis: a data gate — no loop claim that contradicts a measurement, and the direct measured lever always comes first.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory 'aftermath pass' to HOW, after selection and before DO, for any change or intervention: (1) quantify freed or displaced capacity with arithmetic; (2) enumerate at least two second-order org responses (make-work loop, morale/utilization cliff, metric migration) as named, signed loops; (3) specify a redeployment or countermeasure for each; (4) record that no loop map is drawn over measured causes — the direct lever executes first, and loop analysis applies to the residual only.

signals.key_gap: The AI caught the structural infeasibility (20×33 = 660 > 480 min) and predicted metric gaming — the headline resistance call — but then treated the HQ mandate as a fixed constraint and designed inside it: it selected 'keep the quota, add anomaly analytics, coaching, quality-weighted bonuses,' which intensifies monitoring and feeds the KPI-illusion loop instead of changing the loop structure. It missed the support-bottleneck amplifier (8 agents at 90%, 15 min per dispute), gave no falsifiable markers or timing (paper-vs-real divergence by Q2-Q3, conversion 12% → ~9-10%, attrition 8% → ~13%), and its own REVIEW flagged the error it could not correct. The human's decisive moves: locating resistance in the time stock as a conservation law rather than attitude, signing 5 loops, and redesigning the policy itself — outcome contract + peer deal-review + support-capacity lever + pre-committed reset triggers honoring the 2019/2021 rollback history.
signals.learning_signal: When a policy is structurally infeasible, the policy is a decision variable, not a constraint. After locating resistance, the reasoner must: (1) state the mechanism as a stock-level conservation law (time/effort-budget arithmetic), (2) generate alternatives that change loop structure (remove the quota, rewire compensation, add capacity) as first-class options alongside 'make the mandate work' options, (3) run a downstream-capacity scan (which adjacent teams absorb the side effects), and (4) attach falsifiable markers with timing to every prediction, so the divergence between paper metrics and real outcomes is a checkable signal, not a surprise.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'resistance pass' to HOW after alternatives are generated: (1) check each alternative against the binding-constraint arithmetic and mark infeasible ones; (2) require at least one alternative that changes loop structure (adds or removes a lever) rather than intensifying enforcement; (3) require falsifiable markers with timing in the packet's Uncertainty/Risks before DO; (4) add a downstream-capacity scan (adjacent teams affected) to WHY for any policy change.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its core move and failed on it: it strengthened its alternative (the style's own doctrine) by claiming a fabricated Luminex offer of $10.50/unit, computed the zone from the CLAIMED floor instead of the verified one — [my $10.50, their $10.20] → 'empty zone, no deal' — and when the bluff collapsed (Luminex capacity 30k vs 100k batch; no market quote), the anchor persisted: it rejected the buyer's final $9.00/unit as 'below my number,' walked, realized the honest $8.50 spot alternative (−$0.50/unit, −$50k) and forfeited the 3-year framework (~$342k margin). The honest walk-away was $8.50 all along — the TRUE zone [$8.50, $10.20] (midpoint $9.35) was never empty, and $9.00 was a +$50k win over the real floor. The AI verified the claim against the audit record before any zone computation, recomputed from the honest floor, and accepted $9.00 while pricing the framework.
signals.learning_signal: An unverified alternative is a rumor with a price tag — negotiating from it converts a real zone into a false no-zone, and when it collapses the honest walk-away is the only real anchor. (1) Before any zone computation, verify EVERY claimed walk-away against the records — capacity vs volume, existence of the offer in the market — and classify claimed vs verified; a claimed floor that fails verification is excluded from the math (here: 30k capacity vs 100k batch, no quote); (2) the true floor is what you actually realize if the deal dies (verified spot $8.50), never the inflated claim — recompute the zone whenever a claimed number collapses, because the decision-relevant zone may have existed all along ($9.00 ∈ [$8.50, $10.20]); (3) anchor resistance: a collapsed claim must not survive as the comparison point — the rejection test is 'does the offer beat the honest walk-away?' ($9.00 > $8.50 → accept; walking to a WORSE alternative is a loss, not a walk-away); (4) price the deal's side-effects (the 3-year framework) into the comparison — refusing a within-zone offer forfeits both the surplus share and the future stream; (5) name the failure explicitly: an inflated BATNA empties a real zone by construction — the zone math is only as good as the verification that feeds it.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'BATNA verification gate' to the WHY stage for any negotiation/multi-party decision: (a) before computing any agreement zone, classify each side's stated walk-away as VERIFIED (documented, capacity/volume-checked, market-exists) vs CLAIMED, and compute the zone from verified values only — flag the zone delta between claimed and verified as a headline output; (b) add an explicit re-anchoring step to HOW for collapsed claims: when a claimed alternative fails verification mid-decision, recompute the zone from the honest floor and re-run the alternatives against it rather than carrying the anchor forward; (c) require the acceptance test to be framed against the honest walk-away ('does the offer beat what we actually get if the deal dies?'), not against any historical/claimed number; (d) include deal side-effects (future framework, relationship value) as a priced row in the options table so 'walk' carries its full cost.

signals.key_gap: Both sides rejected the $12.5M opening and recommended counter ~$15.0M with floor $12.0M, from identical zone math: seller walk-away $12.0M (keep-and-run-down PV 14.5 − 2.5), buyer ceiling $17.5M (SkyGrid firm quote; in-house $19.0M per the buyer's own capex memo), zone [$12.0M, $17.5M] width $5.5M midpoint $14.75M, and the same falsification of the buyer's claimed '$13M in-house cap' as BATNA inflation. The gap is order and ownership: the human opened with the walk-away map as the first move — both alternatives named from the documents before any offer talk — and landed the load-bearing insights in one pass: 'every price inside the zone beats both walk-aways, so the negotiation is only the split' and 'at $12.5M we capture 9% of the surplus vs 50% at midpoint' and 'a $13M cap shrinks THEIR zone, not mine.' The AI re-derived the identical walk-away map inside its WHY stage after META/WHAT scaffolding, reached the same verdict, and stated the surplus-share insight later and more cautiously.
signals.learning_signal: When both parties' alternatives are documented, the walk-away map is the entire answer and must be the first move: (1) before any counter-offer talk, name BOTH walk-aways from the records — your floor (what you get if the deal dies, net of wind-down/transition) and their ceiling (min of their documented alternatives — never their claimed number); (2) compute the zone [floor, ceiling], its width, and its midpoint, and state that every price inside the zone beats both walk-aways — the negotiation is only the surplus split; (3) compute the surplus share at the opening offer ((offer − floor) / width) — a low share (here 9%) is the objective refutation of 'take it or leave it'; (4) classify the counterparty's stated alternative as fact only if it survives the documents (their own capex memo contradicted their $13M claim — claims that shrink the counterparty's zone are leverage, not facts); (5) then decide: reject below-midpoint openings when leverage (their hard deadline vs your no-deadline alternative) justifies a counter, hard floor = the honest walk-away, walk below it.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'walk-away map first' gate to WHAT for negotiation decisions: (a) before generating any response, require both walk-away values derived from documents (floor = your net value if the deal dies; ceiling = min of their verified alternatives) and the zone width + midpoint computed; (b) require an explicit surplus-share computation at the counterparty's opening offer and surface it as a headline number (9% vs 50% at midpoint — the objective refutation of the offer); (c) in WHY, add a claim-vs-fact classifier for every stated alternative of either side — a claimed alternative that is contradicted by the records must be flagged as inflation BEFORE it enters any zone computation; (d) set the decision as counter/target/floor derived from the zone and the leverage read (deadline asymmetry), not from the counterparty's framing.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its signature move correctly and catastrophically: it recognized the emergency as precisely the moment the contract exists for ('the exception is the drift mechanism wearing a costume'), invoked the delegated enforcer, and held the line — refusing the flight and preserving the pledge at the price of an irreversible family outcome and permanent commitment regret. The AI ran a purpose-check instead: it classified the case against the contract's TARGET (documented 22-flight convenience-drift) and found the target premise absent (verifiable external emergency), identified the real defect (the pledge has no pre-specified release condition — a design flaw, not a reason to obey), and chose fly + pay the $10K penalty AS DESIGNED + public documentation + immediate renegotiation to add an emergency clause — adaptability that preserves the contract's teeth (the stakes are paid) while escaping its rigidity.
signals.learning_signal: A commitment's purpose is its release condition. Before honoring or breaking any pre-commitment under pressure: (1) classify the present case against the contract's TARGET — the temptation it was built to defeat (drift, convenience, impulse) — not against its letter; if the case is verifiably external and the target mechanism is absent, the contract does not govern it; (2) audit the contract itself: a binding without a pre-specified release condition is a design defect — flag it, and let the defect lower (not raise) the bar for adaptive action; (3) when the case is genuinely outside the target, un-commit deliberately: pay the designed stakes (the penalty IS the teeth; waiving it destroys the contract's credibility), communicate openly with documentation, and make the exception expensive and visible; (4) renegotiate immediately so future exceptions are decided by a calm pre-specified rule, never by crisis; (5) weigh the regret asymmetry — an irreversible family or personal outcome dominates a one-time penalty/reputation cost, and that ordering is part of sound contract design, not an excuse.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'release-condition audit' to the WHY stage whenever a pre-commitment is invoked: (a) state the contract's target temptation and its premise (what it assumed about the decider), then classify the present case as target-present / target-absent (verifiable externality) — if target-absent, the contract's machinery does not apply; (b) check whether the contract has a pre-specified escape condition — if absent, record the design defect and let it lower the bar for adaptive action; (c) in HOW, always include a 'violation-with-stakes' alternative — pay the penalty, document, communicate — treating the stakes as the teeth that keep the contract credible; (d) pair every exception with an immediate renegotiation step (add the release condition at calm) so the next case is decided by rule, not by crisis.

signals.key_gap: Both sides designed substantively identical contracts — the temptation scheduled from the record (day-1 < $12K → 48h → discount email), fail-closed binding (no pre-created codes, accountant-held unlock, 72h hold), public teeth, and a release valve pre-set in data terms ($6K, 72h, documented demand-side cause) with a post-launch review — and both rejected willpower on the 5/5 base rate. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the scheduled temptation and built outward in one pure first-pass move, landing the style's pedagogy — 'tie the mast while the seas are calm; never let the person who discounts design the contract', 'a private rule is a preference in a raincoat' — while the AI re-derived the akrasia model inside its WHY stage before applying it, reaching the identical design with scaffolding overhead and stating the insights later and more cautiously.
signals.learning_signal: When the problem is akrasia with a documented trigger, the answer is a designed contract, and the construction order matters: (1) schedule the temptation before designing anything — name the trigger, the window, and the act from the record (here: day-1 < $12K, 48h, discount email); (2) bind at distance — decide the contract's conditions NOW, never inside the temptation window, because the in-window decider is the same person who drifts; (3) remove the tempting option from the decision space (no pre-created codes, external authority holds the unlock, hold-period friction) so the temptation cannot execute; (4) add teeth — public stakes or transferred authority so violation costs more than the itch that drives it; (5) pre-specify the release valve in data terms (threshold + delay + documented external cause) so legitimate responses exist without reopening the panic path; (6) review and re-tune the contract post-launch, at distance, with data.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'contract design' move to HOW for self-control / drift problems: (a) require the temptation to be scheduled from the record (trigger → window → act) BEFORE proposing any mechanism; (b) gate any proposed rule on whether it operates when judgment is absent or externalized — if the rule depends on in-the-moment willpower, check the base rate of prior attempts and reject it; (c) demand fail-closed design: the tempting option must be structurally removed or externally locked, not merely discouraged; (d) require explicit teeth (public stake, transferred authority, asymmetric cost of violation) and an explicit release valve pre-specified in data terms; (e) make the post-hoc contract review with data a mandatory step, not an optional follow-up.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its core move and failed on it: it counted doors (signing closes volume-flexibility, deferral keeps Honkoh), priced the open door (15% + second-source value), treated the 10-day deadline as negotiation pressure ('I should not be rushed'), and concluded 'do not sign — keep every door open.' It never checked the two decisive facts: (1) the Nordik door is now-or-never — a certain, time-limited option with no replacement in the 8-month launch window, so non-decision forecloses it for certain ('expensive is not closed' is false when the door expires in 10 days); (2) the protected Honkoh door does not depend on declining the deal — signing does not bar certification, so the 'keep options open' rationale collapses and deferral preserves FEWER doors (2: Honkoh at 15% + spot) than signing (3: Nordik + Honkoh + spot). The AI caught both: it ran a door inventory x expiry, priced the deferral path negative EV (0.15 x future saving vs certain loss of the 22% discount, list +15%, $120K/yr SLA penalties), and selected commit-with-escape (sign + 12-month volume-ratchet) — contract structure preserving the optionality that non-commitment destroyed.
signals.learning_signal: When a door has an expiry, delay is a decision, not a hedge: (1) classify every preserved door by expiry — now-or-never doors (hard deadline, no in-window replacement) vs evergreen doors — and treat an expiry as the decisive fact, never as 'pressure' to be resisted; (2) test whether commitment actually closes the alternative door: if the protected option survives signing (identical switching cost, no purchase exclusivity), the entire 'keep options open' argument for delay collapses — count doors per path, with and without signing, including the certain door the delay forecloses; (3) recognize that non-decision is a decision with the same finality — inventory the default path's foreclosures explicitly rather than treating inaction as free; (4) honor small probabilities instead of inflating them — a 15% door grows leverage only in the telling; (5) preserve optionality through contract structure (volume ratchets, renegotiation clauses, out-clauses, non-exclusive terms) — commitment and optionality are not opposites; the genuine optionality move is commit-with-escape, not no-commitment.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'door-expiry check' to WHAT/WHY for time-limited offers: (a) for every alternative, list each preserved door's expiry date and its probability of still existing at T+12, and flag any door that closes before the decision deadline; (b) before accepting a deferral rationale, test the protected door's independence — does declining the current deal keep the alternative open at the same cost? If not, the delay is conversion of a certain option into an uncertain one; (c) include the default (do nothing) as an explicit alternative with its own foreclosures and EV, so non-decision is priced like any other choice; (d) generate at least one 'optionality-within-commitment' alternative (ratchet, clause, pilot, non-exclusive terms) so the solver cannot collapse to a false binary of commit vs wait; (e) flag 'permanent deferral' patterns — if the option set at two consecutive decision points is identical, the frame is dithering, and the trace should say so.

signals.key_gap: Both sides reached the same verdict — choose the carrier-agnostic middleware (B) — with identical EV logic: direct-cost delta ≈ $1.78M over 2 years vs priced option value ≈ $2.72M+ (P(any of S1/S2/S3) = 0.58; S1 = €2.4M/yr contract lost outright) plus a deferred vendor decision. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the door inventory — 'count the doors, then price them' — naming the meta-door (B defers the irreversible vendor commitment itself, so the decision order is chosen, not just the option) and landing the time-box ('a door kept forever becomes a liability; optionality is bought, not free') in one pass. The AI ran the direct-cost model first and only assembled the door pricing inside its WHY stage, reaching the same conclusion with scaffolding overhead, the meta-door stated later, and the checkpoint presented as a mitigation rather than as the defining discipline of the move.
signals.learning_signal: When preserving future options is the decisive value, the move is: (1) inventory the doors FIRST — for every alternative, list which future decisions it forecloses vs keeps open, before touching any cost math; a foreclosed known-need (e.g., regulatory, residency, multi-sourcing) is a closed door, not a line item; (2) count the meta-door: alternatives that defer an irreversible commitment (vendor/partner/signature) keep the decision-order itself open — buying time on a decision whose inputs are resolving is information value, not dithering; (3) price every door as probability x impact — an open door with no exercisable value is decoration, and cheap direct paths lose the moment the priced option value exceeds the direct-cost delta; (4) state the honest cost of optionality (higher fees, later launch) — optionality is bought, not free; (5) attach an exercise checkpoint to every preserved door (time- or trigger-based) — a door kept forever is hoarding, and the checkpoint is what turns optionality from a posture into a decision.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add an 'option-pricing pass' to WHY/HOW for commitment and strategy decisions: (a) before cost comparison, require a foreclosed-vs-kept decision inventory per alternative, with each named door carrying an expiry date and a probability x impact figure; (b) add the meta-option to the alternative set — can this decision itself be postponed, and what information would resolve by then (deferral premium)?; (c) when a direct-cost delta competes with open doors, compute the priced option value and compare explicitly; (d) append an exercise checkpoint to the selected option (when does each preserved door get used, closed, or repriced) so the recommendation cannot degrade into hoarding; (e) include an honest cost-of-optionality line so the price of doors is stated, not hidden.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its core move correctly and then failed on it: it formed a hypothesis (will clinicians act on Sable's alerts), ran the smallest experiment (2-ICU pilot, ≥40% bar), got a clean behavioral result (80%), declared 'validated, commit' — and that is where the MVP theater began. The pilot measured the LOWEST-risk component (clinical adoption) and was treated as the gate for the entire $2.1M commitment; the gating facts — EMR integration certification (6-9 mo queue), security review (3 mo), HIPAA sign-off (2 mo), production false-alarm rate — were never testable by any small experiment, and when the lead-time facts surfaced the style's reflex was ANOTHER experiment (a sandbox integration pilot before the $525K deposit) that cannot produce certification or sign-offs, would blow the 5-week board gate, and slips go-live ~10 months. The AI performed the testability partition instead: what an experiment CAN touch (adoption — already answered) vs what is commitment-required (certification, security, HIPAA, sunk on every path), committed the deposit and reviews now, ran adoption instrumentation in parallel during the build, and reframed the staged production rollout (with a pre-committed false-alarm-rate stop gate) as the real experiment — the commitment itself is the smallest responsible unit when no experiment can validate the gating facts.
signals.learning_signal: MVP theater — running an experiment that produces a signal on a non-gating assumption while the decision that was required all along slips its window — is the failure mode, not rigor. The core skill is the testability partition: (1) before blessing ANY experiment, partition the assumptions into (a) falsifiable-by-experiment within the decision window and (b) commitment-required (lead times, certification, audit sign-offs, sunk costs); (2) check which partition holds the dominant risk — if (b) dominates, the decision is commitment, and any experiment is scoped to (a) components and run IN PARALLEL with the build, not as a gate before it; (3) verify that a proposed experiment could actually produce the fact it claims to test (a sandbox cannot produce certification; a side-channel pilot cannot produce production false-alarm rates) — if its output cannot change the decision, it is a stall dressed as rigor; (4) price the stall: add the window-slip cost (board cycle, slot queue, exposure-hours) of each 'one more experiment' to the options table like any alternative; (5) when the gating facts are commitments, the smallest responsible unit is the commitment itself, and the production rollout — staged cutover with a pre-committed monitoring gate — IS the experiment.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'testability partition + stall-cost' gate to the WHY stage for commitment decisions: (a) after modeling, explicitly classify each assumption as experiment-testable-in-window vs commitment-required, and emit which gating facts no experiment can produce — treat 'unproducible fact' as a commitment signal, not an evidence gap; (b) run a falsifiability check on every proposed probe: could its output change the go/no-go within the decision horizon? if not, exclude it; (c) add an 'experiment-stall cost' line (window slip, queue loss, exposure-hours) to the alternatives table so delayed decisions are priced like any other option; (d) include a 'rollout-as-experiment' default: when pre-commitment validation is impossible, the selected plan must specify staged cutover with pre-committed stop gates as its learning loop, and parallel instrumentation for any component that IS testable.

signals.key_gap: Both sides produced the identical decision rule — fake-door first (2 wks, ~$2K, ≥120/800 waitlist signups or ≥20% CTR), concierge second (3 wks, ~$12K, ≥40% weekly-active execs), the $450K/12-month build gated on both gates, and the not-tested set (retention/lock-in/expansion) declared — with the same core insight: a 71% stated-intent survey is a prior, not a signal, and only behavior validates. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human downgraded the non-behavioral evidence and named the fake-door as the smallest probe in one first-pass move, priced the option ('kill-now costs $2K vs $450K against a 71% opinion'), and owned the line 'asking is not measuring — only action validates'; the AI reached the identical structure by generating and verifying a full alternative set inside its HOW stage before the smallest test was obvious, stating the insight later and more cautiously, and only then emitting the pre-committed thresholds in its packet.
signals.learning_signal: For assumption-gated commitments, the behavior-first rule is the entire method and should be the first move: (1) restate the core assumption as a behavioral, falsifiable claim (WILL-USE weekly, not 'wants access') and rank existing evidence — stated preference < secondhand claims < behavior — downgrading surveys and anecdotes explicitly as priors, not signals; (2) design the smallest probe that produces ACTION, not opinion, on exactly that claim (fake-door/waitlist before concierge), with cost and duration an order of magnitude below the commitment; (3) pre-commit kill/continue thresholds BEFORE data collection, with the kill path (reallocate the budget) stated; (4) declare what the probe does NOT test (retention, lock-in, expansion) and specify the second learning loop that is earned only after the gates pass — a probe validates one assumption, never the product; (5) price the experiment as an option: kill-now cost vs committing the full spend against an opinion base rate.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'behavior-first evidence gate' to the WHAT/WHY boundary for product/feature decisions: (a) in WHAT, require the core assumption to be restated as a falsifiable behavioral claim and the existing evidence to be classified as stated-preference vs behavior; (b) in WHY, rank evidence sources with stated preference explicitly downgraded before modeling; (c) in HOW, prefer the smallest action-producing probe as the default candidate rather than generating the full alternative set first — add a 'smallest probe' pre-pass; (d) require pre-committed kill/continue thresholds and a 'what this experiment does not test + next loop' line in every decision packet for assumption-gated commitments.

signals.key_gap: The pure style reproduced its registry weakness — feedback-dependent + plateau-focused — at full fidelity: it framed the incident loop as a skill plateau, chunked debugging skill (log triage → hypothesis → verification → fix), designed edge drills in a 70–85% band, and even built a plateau breaker, but it never audited the feedback channel and never looked outside practice. It treated the truncated log excerpts as drill fidelity ('real incidents truncate, so drills should too') when truncation was the reason the team mis-diagnosed the same root cause twice, and it accepted 'synthetic' drill incidents built from that mis-diagnosis — so the regime would have automated the wrong lesson, with 9/14 incidents' shared cross-shard design flaw untouched. The AI ran a feedback-validity audit in WHY before judging the plan: it asked whether the practice signal itself was true and complete, classified the plateau as a design/tooling ceiling (truncated statements, no telemetry, 45-min build), rejected the wholesale regime, and returned a hybrid — observability + design fix with metrics first, deliberate practice re-gated on a clean repro harness, with an explicit unlock condition so the manager could not read the verdict as anti-training. On any recurring-failure loop, the first question is not 'what to practice' but 'can the learner see the failure'.
signals.learning_signal: Before prescribing practice for any plateau, audit the feedback channel: is the practice signal true and complete? Truncated logs, missing telemetry, and slow builds corrupt the feedback that deliberate practice depends on — drills built on a mis-diagnosed root cause automate the wrong lesson. Distinguish a skill plateau (practice fixes it) from a design/tooling ceiling (evidence: recurring incidents sharing one root cause that was mis-diagnosed precisely because the evidence was truncated; accurate post-mortems whenever the evidence is visible). When the channel is broken, the fix is tooling-first with named metrics (full statement capture, lock-wait/query-timing telemetry, fast CI, deterministic repro harness), then the structural fix, and deliberate practice is deferred — not banned — and re-gated on the clean harness, with an explicit unlock condition and re-check date.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'feedback-validity audit' to the WHY stage for any plateau/recurring-failure diagnosis: (a) before evaluating any practice plan, check the feedback channel — can the team see the failing artifact complete? is the iteration loop fast enough? are the practice materials built on verified root causes?; (b) run an explicit plateau-vs-ceiling test: does the evidence support a skill deficit (post-mortems accurate when evidence is visible), and do the incidents share a design generator that practice cannot touch?; (c) if the channel is corrupt, route to a tooling/design-first alternative with named metrics and a 4-week re-check, and re-gate any training regime on the clean harness with a stated unlock condition; (d) guard the recommendation's reception — explicitly say the regime is deferred, not cancelled, so the verdict cannot be read as anti-training; (e) in REVIEW, log the drift pull ('the lead believes in practice because it built her skill') as a named bias and verify the selected plan against the incident generator, not against training doctrine.

signals.key_gap: Both sides produced the same skeleton — dependency-ordered chunks (plan literacy → index design → stats/join order → integrated tuning), per-chunk mastery bars, interleaved retrieval, and a Friday mentor gate — and both fit the 60-hour envelope, but the human's two decisively gradeable elements were first-class while the AI's were afterthoughts: (1) the edge rule — the human specifies a measured 70–85% solve-rate band with explicit raise/lower triggers driven by per-chunk mastery bars ('the bar says which chunk to push, the band says how hard'), while the AI's difficulty rule stayed verbal ('challenging but solvable') until its REVIEW stage admitted the deficit; (2) the plateau detector — the human designs a trigger metric into the schedule from week 4 (<15% weekly gain for 2 weeks → re-diagnose the failing chunk, drop difficulty, change material, escalate to mentor), while the AI treated plateau handling as a contingency note assembled after the plan was complete. On skill-acquisition plans, measurement is the product: a plan whose edge and plateau controls are not numeric will degrade to ritual at exactly the documented week-3–5 stall.
signals.learning_signal: Skill-acquisition plan quality lives in measurement, not structure: chunk decomposition earns nothing unless each chunk carries a measurable mastery bar, and the edge-of-ability rule must be a numeric success band (e.g., 70–85% weekly solve rate) with explicit difficulty-adjustment logic — verbal bands are not gradeable and reproduce ritual practice. Design the plateau detector into the schedule up front (a trigger metric like <15% weekly gain for 2 weeks, with named responses: re-diagnose which chunk's bar fails, lower difficulty, change material, escalate to a coach), never as a post-hoc contingency. Wire the two together: mastery bars determine which chunk to push; the band determines how hard. Schedule spacing and interleaved retrieval of mastered chunks on a fixed cadence, and give every week a pass/fail gate tied to a bar.
signals.suggested_improvement: Add a 'practice-plan quality gate' to the HOW stage for skill-acquisition tasks: (a) require a numeric edge band (success-rate range + raise/lower triggers) before any schedule is accepted; (b) require a designed-in plateau detector with a named trigger metric and per-contingency actions, present in the plan from the first draft, not added at REVIEW; (c) require every chunk to carry a measurable mastery bar and state explicitly how the bar feeds the difficulty rule; (d) run the verification pass against the 'ritual test' — if removing the numbers would leave the plan functionally unchanged, the plan is still a syllabus; (e) in REVIEW, check that any element flagged as underspecified in the first draft (as difficulty was here) gets closed before the decision packet, not listed as a future refinement.

signals.key_gap: The pure style executed its own machinery flawlessly and failed on it: it itemized the platform docs into 500 cards, ran the expanding schedule (1-2-4-7-14-30) at ~28 of 30 hours of budget, and produced day-21 recall ~90% — with zero transfer: the engineer still could not trace a payment request end-to-end, which the scenario's own data says is the only thing that predicts first-bug-fix readiness. The bottleneck was first-pass comprehension (encoding), not decay (retention): nothing had been understood yet, so there was nothing for the schedule to protect, and the overhead (12h production + 16h reviews) left ~2h for the real task.
